questions.title: Flow Trigger Order at Scale: Before-Save vs. After-Save
questions.prompt: An object has six record-triggered flows plus two Apex triggers. Explain exactly where before-save flows, after-save flows, and Apex triggers each sit in the save order of execution, why that placement matters for performance, and how you decide whether a new piece of logic belongs in a before-save flow, an after-save flow, or Apex.
questions.modelAnswer: Within a single save, Salesforce runs: system validation rules, before-save record-triggered flows (which can update the triggering record's own fields without a second database write), before Apex triggers, custom validation rules, duplicate rules, after-save record-triggered flows, after Apex triggers, assignment rules, auto-response rules, workflow rules (legacy) and their field updates, escalation rules, entitlement rules, roll-up summary recalculation and cross-object workflow, Criteria Based Sharing evaluation, and finally post-commit logic like Einstein/async Apex and output from after-save flows that touch other records. Before-save flows are cheapest because they modify the in-memory record before it's committed, avoiding a second DML and re-firing of the save pipeline. After-save flows, by contrast, always re-save the record (or related records), which re-triggers the entire pipeline again, including other automation on the affected object, so they're inherently more expensive and the ones most likely to cause recursion. The decision rule: if the logic only sets fields on the triggering record itself with no related-record DML and no external callout, it belongs in a before-save flow. If it needs to create or update other records, send an email, or call a subflow that does either, it has to be after-save. If it needs to call out synchronously, enforce complex multi-object validation Flow can't express cleanly, or needs unit-testable, version-controlled logic for compliance reasons, it belongs in Apex instead of either flow type.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd draw the save order out for them rather than just listing it, because the placement is the whole point. Before-save flows run first and they're basically free — they edit the record that's about to be saved before it's written, so there's no extra trip to the database. After-save flows run later, and critically, anything they touch gets saved separately, which means the whole order-of-execution pipeline fires again for that DML. That's why six flows plus two triggers on one object makes me nervous — if even one of those after-save flows updates a field that a before-save flow or trigger reacts to, I've got a recursion risk. So my rule of thumb is boring on purpose: if it's just setting a field on the same record, before-save, every time. The moment it touches a different record or sends something external, it has to be after-save, and if the logic is genuinely complex — multi-object, needs a callout, needs to be unit tested for an audit — that's when I pull it into Apex instead of stacking a seventh flow on top of the six that are already there.
commonMistakes: Doesn't know before-save flows avoid a second DML while after-save flows trigger a full re-save
Treats all record-triggered flows as running at the same point in the save order
Puts same-record-only field updates in an after-save flow for no reason, adding unnecessary DML
Has no concrete rule for when logic should move to Apex instead of another flow
keyPoints: Correctly sequences before-save flows, Apex triggers, validation rules, and after-save flows
Explains why before-save flows are cheaper (no second DML)
Explains why after-save flows re-trigger the save pipeline and raise recursion risk
Gives a concrete decision rule for before-save vs. after-save vs. Apex

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the order of execution and where each automation type sits
Explains the performance difference between before-save and after-save flows
Gives a clear, defensible rule for choosing between before-save, after-save, and Apex

questions.title: Flow vs. Apex: An Enterprise Governance Decision, Not a Preference
questions.prompt: A junior admin argues every automation should be built in Flow because 'that's the declarative-first principle,' while a developer on the team argues everything complex should just be Apex for control and testability. As the person who owns the automation standard for the org, how do you actually decide, case by case, and what does your written standard say?
questions.modelAnswer: Both positions are oversimplified rules standing in for a real decision framework. 'Declarative-first' is a good default because flows are visible to every admin, version through metadata the same way, and don't need a developer to maintain — but it breaks down past a certain complexity, data volume, or testability requirement. The written standard should define concrete triggers for escalating to Apex: when logic needs transaction-level control (e.g., partial rollback of related records that Flow's fault paths can't cleanly express), when it needs genuinely unit-testable business logic for a regulated process, when performance at high data volumes requires bulkified SOQL/DML patterns beyond what Flow's native bulkification gives you, or when the same logic needs to be reused across both UI and API entry points where a single Apex class is cleaner than a flow plus Apex-invoked-from-flow wrapper. Conversely, Apex should not be the default for things Flow handles natively — field updates, simple approval routing, screen-driven data entry — because that creates a maintenance burden only developers can touch and removes the audit trail admins can read directly in Flow Builder. The standard should also require that any decision to use Apex be documented with the specific limitation that forced it, so the next person doesn't have to re-litigate the decision.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell both of them the same thing: neither 'always Flow' nor 'always Apex' is a standard, it's a slogan, and I'm not writing either one into our governance doc. What I actually put in writing is a short list of specific triggers that push something into Apex — needing real transaction control, needing unit tests for a compliance-sensitive process, hitting a data volume or complexity ceiling Flow's bulkification can't absorb cleanly, or needing the same logic callable from both a flow and an API integration. If none of those apply, it's Flow, full stop, because that keeps the automation visible and maintainable by the whole admin team, not just whoever wrote the Apex. And when something does go to Apex, I require a one-line note in the class header saying which of those triggers justified it, so six months from now nobody has to re-argue this exact disagreement from scratch.
commonMistakes: Picks a side (always Flow or always Apex) instead of a decision framework
Doesn't name concrete technical triggers for escalating to Apex
Ignores the maintainability cost of Apex for things admins could own declaratively
No mechanism to document why a given automation landed where it did
keyPoints: Rejects both absolute positions as oversimplified
Names specific, concrete criteria for when Apex is justified
Explains the maintainability/visibility cost of defaulting to Apex
Requires documentation of the decision for future maintainers

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Rejects both oversimplified positions and proposes a real framework
Names concrete, technically sound triggers for choosing Apex
Addresses maintainability and visibility tradeoffs
Builds documentation/governance into the standard itself

questions.title: Writing a Declarative-Automation Standard for a 200-Flow Org
questions.prompt: Your org has grown to roughly 200 flows across 30 objects, built by a rotating cast of admins and contractors over several years, with no naming convention and overlapping triggers on several key objects. What does a written declarative-automation standard need to cover to make this maintainable going forward, and how would you roll it out without freezing the business?
questions.modelAnswer: A real standard needs at minimum: a naming convention that encodes object, trigger type, and purpose so a flow's name alone tells you what it does and when it runs (e.g., Object_BeforeSave_Purpose); a hard rule limiting the number of record-triggered flows per object per save context (ideally one before-save and one after-save flow per object, using decision elements inside that single flow to branch logic, rather than many competing flows whose relative order is implicit and hard to reason about); mandatory fault-path handling on every flow that performs DML; a documentation requirement (a description field populated on every flow and a change log of what changed and why); and a review/approval gate before any new flow ships to production, similar to a code review. Rolling this out without freezing the business means it can't be a stop-everything rewrite: start by applying the new standard to every new flow going forward (zero cost to existing work), then triage existing flows by risk — objects with the most overlapping automation and highest change frequency get consolidated first — and schedule that consolidation as its own tracked project with regression testing, not as an afterthought squeezed into unrelated feature work. Communicate the standard in a short, concrete one-pager, not a long policy document nobody reads, and make compliance visible (a dashboard of flows that are and aren't documented) so it's self-reinforcing rather than relying on individual admins remembering a rule.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't start by rewriting 200 flows — that's how you blow a budget and still not finish. I'd start by writing down, in one page, the handful of rules that actually prevent this problem from getting worse: a naming convention that tells you the object, the trigger timing, and the purpose just from the name; a hard cap of one before-save and one after-save flow per object, with branching inside that single flow instead of five competing flows; required fault paths on anything that writes data; and a lightweight review step before anything new goes live, the same way we'd code-review anything else. That standard applies immediately to new work, at zero cost. Then I'd triage the existing 200 — the handful of objects with the most overlapping flows and the highest change frequency get consolidated first, as its own scoped project with real regression testing, not bolted onto whatever feature work is already in flight. And I'd make the standard visible, not just written — a simple report of which flows are and aren't following it — because a rule nobody can see compliance against just quietly stops being followed.
commonMistakes: Proposes rewriting all 200 flows at once instead of a phased, risk-based approach
No concrete naming convention, just 'be consistent'
Doesn't cap or consolidate overlapping flows per object
No ongoing visibility/enforcement mechanism once the standard is written
keyPoints: Defines a concrete naming convention tied to object, trigger timing, and purpose
Caps flows per object per trigger context to reduce overlap and ordering ambiguity
Requires fault-path handling and documentation as non-negotiable
Phases rollout: new work first, then risk-based consolidation of existing flows
Makes ongoing compliance visible rather than relying on memory

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a concrete, specific standard (naming, caps, fault handling, documentation)
Phases the rollout realistically without freezing the business
Prioritizes consolidation by risk rather than doing everything at once
Builds in ongoing visibility/enforcement

questions.title: Governor Limits in Flow at Enterprise Scale
questions.prompt: A nightly batch process updates 40,000 Opportunity records, and each update re-fires an after-save flow that performs a Get Records call against a related object. Walk through which governor limits are actually at risk here, why bulkification in Flow doesn't fully protect you the way it does in a well-written Apex trigger, and how you'd redesign this.
questions.modelAnswer: The limits actually at risk are the SOQL query limit (100 synchronous / 200 asynchronous queries per transaction) and total heap/CPU time, because Flow does bulkify DML and, for Get Records placed directly in the flow, it also bulkifies the query across all records in a given transaction chunk — but that bulking only works cleanly when the Get Records element's filter can be satisfied by a single query across the whole batch. If the flow's logic forces a Get Records call that depends on a value computed per-record inside a loop (a very common anti-pattern), Flow can't merge those into one query, and you get one SOQL call per record, which exhausts the 100-query synchronous limit well before 40,000 records are processed — the batch update will get chunked into transactions of 200 records by the Bulk API, but 200 individual per-record queries still blows the limit instantly. The fix is to restructure the flow so any Get Records call sits outside loops entirely, querying with an 'is in collection' filter against a collection built once per transaction, then using an in-memory loop with lookups against that already-retrieved collection instead of re-querying per record. If the related-record logic is inherently too complex to express that way declaratively, this is exactly the kind of case where moving the logic into a bulkified Apex trigger (one query, one map lookup per record) is the architecturally correct answer, not a workaround.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd check is where that Get Records element actually sits in the flow, because that's the whole story. If it's inside a loop, Flow has no way to combine it with the other 39,999 — each one fires on its own, and you'll blow through the SOQL limit almost immediately, way before you get anywhere near 40,000 records. Flow's bulkification is real, but it only works for filters it can express as one query across the batch; the moment the filter value is something computed per record inside a loop, that guarantee is gone. So my redesign is: pull that Get Records element out of the loop entirely, query once for the whole collection using an 'is in' filter, and then do the per-record matching in memory against that collection instead of hitting the database again for every single row. And if the logic genuinely can't be restructured that way — if it really does need a different query shape per record — that's not a sign to fight Flow harder, that's the signal to hand this specific piece to Apex, where a bulkified SOQL-plus-map pattern handles exactly this case cleanly.
commonMistakes: Assumes Flow automatically bulkifies every Get Records call regardless of placement
Doesn't identify a Get Records call inside a loop as the actual root cause
Proposes raising limits or splitting the batch smaller instead of restructuring the query
Treats moving to Apex as giving up rather than the architecturally correct escalation
keyPoints: Identifies the SOQL governor limit as the actual risk, not DML
Explains that Flow bulkification breaks down when Get Records sits inside a loop
Proposes moving Get Records outside the loop with an 'is in collection' filter
Recognizes when the correct fix is escalating to a bulkified Apex pattern instead

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the governor limit actually at risk and why
Explains the specific anti-pattern (query inside a loop) causing the failure
Proposes a concrete, correct redesign (query outside the loop, in-memory matching)
Recognizes when the right answer is escalating to Apex

questions.title: Flow Orchestration vs. a Pile of Individual Flows
questions.prompt: Explain what Flow Orchestration actually adds that a well-designed autolaunched flow calling several subflows doesn't already give you, and describe a real multi-step business process where orchestration is the better architectural choice.
questions.modelAnswer: A autolaunched flow calling subflows executes everything in one continuous transaction context, synchronously (or as one background run), with no native concept of pausing for a different person's action on a different day, no built-in stage tracking, and no per-step assignment to different users or queues. Flow Orchestration is purpose-built for multi-step, multi-person, multi-day processes: it introduces Stages and Steps that can be assigned to specific users or queues, can pause and wait for a human to complete an Interactive Step (a screen flow) at their own pace, and gives you a visual, trackable record of where a given case sits in the process without custom status fields and reporting built by hand. A real example: a complex customer-offboarding process that requires a sales rep to confirm contract terms, then legal to review and approve a termination clause, then finance to process a final invoice, then an automated step to deactivate licenses — each step done by a different role, on a different timeline, sometimes with days between them. Chaining that as subflows inside one autolaunched flow would require you to hand-build status tracking, task assignment, and reentry logic yourself; Orchestration gives you that structure natively, with a clear visual map of the process that both admins and the business can read. For short, single-transaction logic with no human waiting involved, plain subflows remain simpler and are the better choice — orchestration adds real overhead that isn't worth it for something that completes in one run.
questions.professionalAnswer: The honest answer is: for anything that finishes in one transaction, orchestration is overkill, and I'd just use an autolaunched flow with subflows for readability. Where orchestration actually earns its place is when the process spans people and time — when step two can't happen until a human in a completely different department does something, maybe days later. A good example is customer offboarding: sales confirms terms, legal reviews a termination clause, finance processes the final invoice, then licenses get deactivated automatically — four steps, three different roles, no guarantee any of them happen the same day. Trying to force that into subflows means I'm hand-building my own status field, my own 'who does this belong to right now' logic, and my own reporting on where every case is stuck. Orchestration gives me stages and steps that assign themselves to the right person or queue, pause cleanly waiting for their input, and show me a visual map of exactly where every case in flight actually is. I'd pick orchestration specifically because the process has human waiting time built into it, not because it sounds more advanced than subflows.
commonMistakes: Treats Orchestration as simply 'subflows but fancier' without naming the human-pause/stage mechanism
Recommends Orchestration for a single-transaction process where it adds unnecessary overhead
Doesn't give a concrete, multi-day, multi-role example process
Ignores the native status tracking/reporting value Orchestration provides over hand-built fields
keyPoints: Explains Stages, Steps, and per-step user/queue assignment as the real differentiator
Explains that Orchestration natively pauses across days for human input, unlike plain subflows
Gives a concrete multi-role, multi-day example process
Correctly scopes when plain subflows remain the simpler, better choice

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what Orchestration adds (stages, steps, pausing, assignment)
Gives a concrete, well-reasoned example process where it's the right fit
Correctly scopes when plain subflows are still the better, simpler choice

questions.title: Preventing Recursion Across Six Flows on the Same Object
questions.prompt: Six different record-triggered flows run on the Case object, several of them updating fields that other flows in the set also watch for changes. Explain the actual mechanisms Flow provides to prevent infinite or wasteful recursion in this situation, and which one you'd reach for first.
questions.modelAnswer: The core problem is that any after-save flow which updates a field another flow is triggered by causes that second flow to fire again, and if that second flow in turn updates something the first one watches, you get a loop that only governor limits (or Salesforce's internal recursion guard on the same record within a transaction) eventually stop — and even where it stops rather than erroring, every extra pass burns limits for nothing. The primary prevention mechanism is entry-condition discipline: every record-triggered flow should have 'Run the flow only when a record is updated to meet the condition requirements' set, with entry criteria specific enough that the flow doesn't re-fire on its own resulting update (for example, checking that a Stage field changed to a new value, rather than firing on any save of the record). The second mechanism is consolidation: rather than six flows independently watching overlapping fields, merge logic that reacts to the same trigger context into fewer flows with internal decision branching, which makes the actual dependency graph visible and auditable instead of implicit across six separate automations. The third, more surgical mechanism is a recursion-guard flag — a formula or a transaction-scoped indicator checked at entry — used when the first two approaches aren't sufficient for a genuinely interdependent pair of updates. I'd reach for tightened entry conditions first, because it's the cheapest fix and forces you to actually understand what each flow is reacting to; consolidation is the real long-term architectural fix once the immediate risk is contained.
questions.professionalAnswer: Six flows on one object with overlapping field updates is exactly the setup that causes the recursion incidents I've had to clean up before, so I'd treat this as urgent. First thing I'd check on every one of the six: does the entry condition actually say 'only run when this specific field changes to this specific value,' or does it just say 'record is updated' — because the second one is how a flow ends up re-triggering itself through its own downstream effects. Tightening entry conditions is step one because it's fast and it forces me to actually map out who's reacting to what. Longer term, I don't want six independently-evolving flows implicitly depending on each other's side effects — I'd consolidate the ones reacting to the same trigger context into fewer flows with branching logic inside, so the dependency is visible in one place instead of inferred across six screens. If there's a genuinely circular pair of updates that can't be untangled that way, that's when I'd add an explicit recursion-guard check at the top of the flow rather than hoping entry conditions alone catch it.
commonMistakes: Assumes Salesforce fully prevents recursion automatically with no admin action needed
Doesn't tighten entry conditions to specific field-value transitions
Treats six separate flows as fine as long as nothing is currently broken
Never mentions consolidating overlapping automation as the durable architectural fix

Names tightened entry conditions as the primary, cheapest defense
Proposes consolidating overlapping flows to make dependencies visible
Mentions an explicit recursion-guard mechanism for genuinely circular cases

Prioritizes entry-condition tightening as the first, cheapest fix

questions.title: Territory Management vs. Role Hierarchy for Record Access
questions.prompt: A sales organization is restructuring around overlapping geographic and product-line territories, and the current role hierarchy alone can't model who should see which Accounts. Explain conceptually how Enterprise/Territory Management changes the access model compared to role hierarchy and sharing rules alone, and when it's actually justified over a simpler sharing-rule-based design.
questions.modelAnswer: Role hierarchy and sharing rules grant access based on a user's static position in the org chart or static criteria on a record, which works well when 'who should see this Account' maps cleanly onto 'who manages this person' or 'what region this Account is tagged with.' Territory Management introduces a separate hierarchy specifically for assigning accounts (and their related opportunities, if enabled) based on multiple, independent, possibly overlapping criteria — a given Account can sit in both a geographic territory and a product-line territory simultaneously, each granting access to a different team, which a single role hierarchy fundamentally cannot express since a record only reports to one place in that hierarchy. Territory Management also supports rule-based automatic assignment of accounts to territories as attributes change, rather than requiring a manually maintained sharing rule for every combination. It's justified specifically when accounts need to be visible to multiple, independently-structured teams at once based on different dimensions (geography and product line both legitimately needing access), when territory assignment needs to change automatically as account attributes change, and when the organization's sales model genuinely overlays multiple structures rather than a single clean hierarchy. It is overkill, and meaningfully more complex to maintain, for an org where sharing-rule criteria based on a single field (region, or owner's role) already captures who needs access — in that simpler case, territory management adds setup, forecasting, and reporting complexity without a corresponding access-modeling benefit.
questions.professionalAnswer: The honest framing is that role hierarchy answers one question well — who's above whom — and that's not actually the question this org has anymore, because an Account now legitimately needs to be visible to both a geographic team and a separate product-line team, and a role hierarchy can only put that Account in one place. Territory Management exists for exactly that overlap: it lets the same Account live in more than one territory at once, each with its own access grant, and it can reassign accounts automatically as attributes change instead of someone maintaining sharing rules by hand for every combination. But I wouldn't reach for it just because the requirements sound complicated — if a straightforward sharing rule based on region or the owner's role already gets the right people access, territory management is genuinely more setup and more ongoing maintenance, especially once you factor in forecasting and territory-based reporting, for no real gain. I'd only recommend it here because the requirement is specifically 'multiple independent, overlapping structures need simultaneous access,' which is the one thing role hierarchy and sharing rules alone can't do.
commonMistakes: Treats Territory Management as just 'a bigger role hierarchy'
Doesn't explain that an Account can belong to multiple territories simultaneously
Recommends Territory Management without checking if simpler sharing rules would suffice
Ignores the ongoing maintenance and forecasting complexity Territory Management introduces
keyPoints: Explains that role hierarchy only models a single reporting structure per record
Explains Territory Management's ability to grant access via multiple overlapping territories
Names rule-based automatic territory assignment as a real capability gap vs. sharing rules
Correctly scopes when the simpler sharing-rule approach is still the better choice

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the conceptual gap role hierarchy/sharing rules can't fill
Correctly explains what Territory Management adds (multi-territory, auto-assignment)
Gives a defensible standard for when it's justified vs. overkill

questions.title: Sharing Sets and Guest/Community User Access, Conceptually
questions.prompt: A partner community needs external users to see only the Accounts and Cases tied to their own company, while internal staff need the full internal sharing model untouched. Explain conceptually how sharing sets differ from standard sharing rules, and why community/guest access needs its own deliberate design rather than reusing internal sharing rules.
questions.modelAnswer: Standard sharing rules grant access based on a user's role, group, or a criteria match, assuming the user is an internal, licensed user who sits somewhere in the org's role hierarchy — external community or portal users typically don't have a meaningful position in that hierarchy, so standard role-based sharing rules don't apply to them the same way. Sharing Sets solve the specific problem of giving an external user access to records based on a mapping between an attribute on their own User/Contact/Account record and a matching attribute on the target record — for example, 'grant access to any Case where the Case's Account equals the external user's own Account' — without having to build a custom role hierarchy branch for every external account. This is deliberately narrower and more mechanical than internal sharing rules, which is exactly the point: external access needs to be airtight and self-limiting by construction, because a mistake here exposes data to people outside the company, not just to the wrong internal department. Guest user access (for unauthenticated visitors on a public-facing community page) is an even more restrictive case that deserves its own explicit review, since guest users have no login at all and historically have been a common source of accidental over-exposure when the same object permissions used for authenticated community users were mistakenly left open to guests too. The deliberate-design principle is: never assume internal sharing logic generalizes to external users; build and test external access as its own explicit, minimal-by-default model.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mental model I'd give the team is that internal sharing rules assume the person has a real place in our org chart, and external partner users just don't — there's no role hierarchy position for 'Acme Corp's support contact,' so reusing internal sharing rules for them doesn't actually work as a strategy. Sharing Sets exist specifically for this: you say 'this external user can see any Case whose Account matches their own Account,' and Salesforce enforces that mapping without me building a custom hierarchy branch per partner company. I'd treat guest user access as its own separate, even more cautious conversation, because guest users aren't logged in at all, and I've seen real orgs accidentally expose record data to the public internet because someone assumed the same object permission that was fine for authenticated community users was also fine for guests. So my actual plan here: use Sharing Sets to map partner users to their own company's records, leave internal sharing rules completely untouched since they're solving a different problem for a different population, and do a dedicated access review specifically on what the guest profile can see before this community page goes anywhere near production.

Doesn't explain the actual mapping mechanism Sharing Sets use (user attribute to record attribute)
Treats guest user access as the same risk level as authenticated community user access
No mention of a dedicated access review before a community/guest-facing page ships

Correctly explains the Sharing Set attribute-matching mechanism
Treats guest (unauthenticated) access as a distinct, higher-risk case requiring its own review
Recommends minimal-by-default external access design rather than reusing internal logic

Correctly explains the Sharing Set mechanism

questions.title: Apex Managed Sharing, Conceptually
questions.prompt: A business rule for who can see an Opportunity depends on logic too dynamic for a standard sharing rule to express (it depends on a calculation across several related records, not a static field match). Explain, conceptually, what Apex managed sharing is, how it differs from a sharing rule, and what the ongoing cost of choosing it actually looks like.
questions.modelAnswer: A standard sharing rule evaluates a static criteria match or a role/group membership and Salesforce maintains the resulting share records automatically whenever the underlying criteria change. Apex managed sharing is a share record your own code creates and owns directly, used specifically when the access decision depends on logic a declarative sharing rule's criteria builder can't express — a calculation across multiple related records, an external system's determination, or a rule with branching logic that isn't a simple field comparison. The critical difference in ongoing cost is ownership: because the sharing rule is 'managed' by Apex rather than by Salesforce's own rule engine, your code is now responsible for creating the share record when access should be granted and for removing it when the underlying condition changes and access should be revoked — nothing automatically keeps the share record in sync with the business logic the way a standard sharing rule does. That means every event that could change the eligibility calculation needs code (likely a trigger or scheduled job) that re-evaluates and corrects sharing, and a bug in that logic leaves stale over- or under-sharing in place silently, since nothing will flag it as wrong. I'd only reach for this after confirming the access logic genuinely can't be expressed as a criteria-based or owner-based sharing rule, and I'd insist on automated tests covering both the grant and the revoke path, not just the grant.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I'd frame it to the team: a normal sharing rule is something Salesforce babysits for you — the criteria change, the share record updates itself, you don't think about it again. Apex managed sharing means we're the babysitter now. We only reach for it because the access decision genuinely can't be written as a criteria match — it depends on a calculation across related records that a rule builder just can't express. But the moment we write that share record ourselves, we also own un-sharing it the moment the condition stops being true, and that's the part teams forget. If the trigger or scheduled job that revokes access has a bug, nothing tells us — the record just stays visible to someone who shouldn't see it anymore, silently, until someone notices in an audit. So before I sign off on this approach, I want to see confidence that we really can't express this as a standard rule, and I want test coverage on the revoke path specifically, not just the grant path, because that's where I've seen these quietly rot.
commonMistakes: Doesn't distinguish Apex managed sharing from standard sharing rules in terms of who maintains the share record
Ignores that the revoke path is entirely the developer's responsibility, with no automatic correction
Jumps to Apex managed sharing without confirming a standard sharing rule genuinely can't express the logic
No mention of testing the revoke path specifically
keyPoints: Explains that Apex managed sharing is a share record owned and maintained by custom code
Explains that nothing automatically revokes access when the underlying condition changes
Identifies the ongoing maintenance/testing burden this creates
Confirms standard sharing rules should be ruled out first

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what Apex managed sharing is and how it differs from sharing rules
Correctly explains the ongoing maintenance burden (grant AND revoke)
Appropriately scopes it as a last resort after ruling out declarative options

questions.title: Why a Role Hierarchy Change Triggers a Slow, Org-Wide Sharing Recalculation
questions.prompt: Changing a single role's position in the role hierarchy on a large org can trigger a sharing recalculation that takes hours and affects performance org-wide. Explain what's actually happening under the hood during that recalculation, and the concrete steps you'd take before making a role hierarchy change on a production org with millions of records.
questions.modelAnswer: Salesforce's sharing model maintains implicit share records (reflected in tables like GroupMember and the object's Share table) that encode exactly who can see which record based on ownership, role hierarchy position, and sharing rules — this isn't recalculated live on every query, it's materialized ahead of time so that read performance stays fast. Moving a role in the hierarchy changes which roles are 'above' which other roles for grant-access-using-hierarchies purposes, which means every record owned by every user under the moved role (and every sharing rule that references role-based groups) potentially needs its share records regenerated to reflect the new structure — on an org with millions of records, that's a full recalculation job touching a very large number of share rows, run asynchronously, and it can genuinely take hours and compete with other background processes for Apex/async capacity. Before making a role hierarchy change on a production org at that scale, I would: make the change during the lowest-traffic maintenance window available, notify stakeholders that reports and some record access may lag temporarily during recalculation, check Setup's sharing recalculation / async job monitor beforehand to confirm no other large job is already queued that would compete for capacity, and seriously consider whether the business need can be met with a sharing rule or public group change instead of a role hierarchy move, since the latter is the single most expensive sharing-model change available and should be treated as a last resort for large orgs, not a routine org-chart edit.
questions.professionalAnswer: What's actually happening is that Salesforce doesn't figure out who can see a record at query time — it pre-computes that into share tables so reads stay fast, and a role hierarchy move changes the inputs to that computation for every single user under the role that moved, and for every sharing rule that leans on role-based groups. On an org with millions of records that's not a quick update, it's a full recalculation job, and it's going to eat async capacity for potentially hours. So before I'd touch a role hierarchy on a production org that size, I'm doing a few things: scheduling it for the lowest-traffic window we have, telling stakeholders up front that access and some reports might lag while it processes, checking the job monitor to make sure I'm not stacking this on top of another big async job already running, and — honestly — asking whether we actually need to move the role at all, or whether a sharing rule or public group change gets us the same access outcome without triggering the single most expensive operation in the sharing model. I'd treat a role hierarchy move as a scheduled, planned change, never a quick Tuesday-afternoon tweak.

Doesn't connect the role move to every user under that role needing recalculation
Treats the change as routine with no maintenance-window planning
Doesn't consider a sharing rule or public group change as a less expensive alternative

Explains why a role move cascades to every user under that role and related sharing rules
Plans the change around a maintenance window and checks for competing async jobs
Considers a cheaper alternative (sharing rule/public group) before moving the role

questions.title: Large Data Volume Considerations Before They Become a Crisis
questions.prompt: An org is projected to grow a custom object from 2 million to 40 million records over the next two years. What specific large-data-volume (LDV) considerations do you raise now, before that growth happens, rather than after performance problems start?
questions.modelAnswer: At LDV scale, several things that are invisible at 2 million rows become first-order design constraints: selective SOQL filtering becomes mandatory, because the query optimizer needs an indexed, selective filter (generally under roughly 10% of a very large table, tighter than the simpler rule of thumb at smaller scale) to avoid a full table scan, so any report or flow Get Records call relying on a non-indexed or low-selectivity field will degrade sharply as the table grows. Record ownership skew matters more — a single user or a single queue owning a disproportionate share of records (ownership skew) slows down any operation that recalculates sharing for that owner, and the common mitigation is spreading ownership or using a dedicated 'skinny' owner strategy. Lookup skew (one record being referenced by millions of child records) causes similar lock contention during bulk updates to the parent. Indexing strategy needs active review — custom indexes (via a case with Salesforce support, or Admin-managed external IDs/unique fields) on the fields actually used for filtering become necessary rather than optional. Bulk data operations need to move to the Bulk API with properly sized batches and PK chunking for extracts, rather than ad hoc Data Loader runs sized for the current volume. And archiving/retention policy needs to be decided now — deciding what, if anything, gets archived off the primary object (via Big Objects, an external archive, or deletion policy) is far cheaper to design before the growth happens than to retrofit once reports and page loads are already struggling under the full 40 million rows.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd raise this now specifically because every fix here is cheap today and expensive in eighteen months. First, I'd look hard at what fields reports, flows, and list views are actually filtering on, because at 40 million rows a non-selective filter doesn't just get slower, it falls off a cliff into a full table scan — so I want the right custom indexes in place before that matters, not after someone opens a ticket about a report timing out. Second, I'd ask about ownership patterns — if one queue or one integration user is going to end up owning a huge share of those records, that's ownership skew, and it makes sharing recalculation and bulk updates on that owner's records noticeably slower; better to spread that out by design now than reshuffle 40 million records later. Third, bulk operations need to already be built on the Bulk API with sensible batch sizes, not on Data Loader settings that happen to work fine at 2 million rows. And fourth, I'd force the retention conversation now — does every one of those 40 million rows need to live on the primary object forever, or do we design an archiving strategy today, while it's a design decision, instead of a frantic migration project later.
commonMistakes: Doesn't mention SOQL selectivity/indexing thresholds specific to large tables
Doesn't address ownership or lookup skew
Assumes current Data Loader/API approach scales linearly with no changes needed
No mention of archiving or retention strategy
keyPoints: Explains SOQL selectivity and indexing requirements at large scale
Addresses ownership skew and lookup skew as concrete LDV risks
Recommends Bulk API strategy appropriate to the eventual data volume
Raises archiving/retention strategy as a proactive design decision

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains selectivity/indexing concerns at LDV scale
Addresses ownership and/or lookup skew
Addresses bulk operation strategy appropriate to the volume
Raises archiving/retention as a proactive decision

questions.title: Skinny Tables, Conceptually: What They Fix and What They Don't
questions.prompt: A performance review recommends asking Salesforce support for a skinny table on a large, frequently-reported-on custom object. Explain conceptually what a skinny table is, what specific kind of slowness it addresses, and what it does nothing for.
questions.modelAnswer: Conceptually, a skinny table is a narrower, denormalized copy of a subset of an object's fields that Salesforce maintains automatically in sync with the base table, used specifically to speed up read-heavy operations like reports and list views that only need a handful of frequently-accessed fields rather than the full row. By avoiding joins against the base object's full schema (including fields stored in separate extension tables once an object has very many custom fields) and avoiding soft-deleted-row filtering overhead on every read, a skinny table can measurably speed up exactly the queries it's built to serve: large reports, list views, and SOQL filtered on the fields included in that skinny table. What it does nothing for: it doesn't help write performance (inserts/updates still go through the base object and its full set of triggers, flows, and validation, and the skinny table is just kept in sync afterward), it doesn't help queries that need fields not included in it (you fall straight back to the base table), and it's not a substitute for proper indexing or selective filters — a non-selective query against a skinny table can still scan slowly. It also requires a support case to provision and maintain (it's not self-service), and has a field-count ceiling, so it's a targeted tool for a specific, already-diagnosed read-performance problem on a known, stable set of fields, not a general-purpose fix you reach for before you've actually confirmed where the slowness is coming from.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd want to make sure we're asking for the right thing before we file that support case. A skinny table is really just a narrow, read-optimized copy of a handful of fields that Salesforce keeps in sync for us, and it helps exactly one kind of problem: reports, list views, and SOQL that only need those specific fields and are currently paying for joins against the full object — including the extension tables that show up once an object has a lot of custom fields. It does nothing for writes; every insert and update still goes through the real object, triggers and all, and the skinny table just catches up afterward. And it does nothing if the slow query needs a field that isn't in the skinny table, or if the real problem is a non-selective filter — a skinny table doesn't fix bad filtering, it just makes a well-filtered query faster. So before I recommend this, I want an actual diagnosis showing the slow reports consistently use the same narrow set of fields — otherwise we file a support case, wait for provisioning, and the reports are still slow because we fixed the wrong layer.
commonMistakes: Describes a skinny table as a general performance fix rather than a targeted read optimization
Doesn't mention it requires a Salesforce support case to provision
Claims it helps write performance
Doesn't note it only helps queries actually using its included fields
keyPoints: Correctly explains a skinny table as a synced, denormalized read-optimized copy
Explains the specific read scenarios it speeds up (avoiding joins/extension tables)
Correctly states it does not help writes or non-selective queries
Notes it requires Salesforce support provisioning and a prior diagnosis

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what a skinny table is and how it's maintained
Correctly explains what it actually speeds up
Correctly explains its limitations (writes, missing fields, non-selective queries)

questions.title: Choosing a Bulk API Strategy for a Nightly 5-Million-Row Integration
questions.prompt: An integration needs to upsert roughly 5 million records every night from an external ERP system. Walk through the Bulk API strategy decisions involved — batch sizing, parallel vs. serial processing mode, and how you'd avoid lock contention — and why Data Loader's default settings wouldn't hold up here.
questions.modelAnswer: At 5 million rows a night, the integration needs the Bulk API (v1 or v2) rather than the standard SOAP/REST API, because Bulk API is purpose-built for asynchronous, large-batch processing with much higher throughput per call. Batch sizing matters: Bulk API v2 handles chunking into roughly 10,000-record batches automatically, but v1 requires you to size batches deliberately — too small wastes overhead per batch, too large risks timeouts and makes a single bad record's error harder to isolate within the batch. Parallel vs. serial processing mode is the critical decision for this specific scenario: parallel mode processes batches concurrently for speed, but if the 5 million records include many updates to the same parent record (for example, many line-item-style child records all rolling up to a shared parent), parallel batches can lock against each other trying to update related records simultaneously, causing failures and retries that cost more time than they save; serial mode processes batches one at a time, trading raw throughput for eliminating that lock contention. Given a nightly ERP sync almost certainly has exactly this kind of relational skew (orders referencing shared accounts, line items referencing shared products), I'd default to serial mode unless testing proves the data is free of that overlap. Data Loader's default settings fall over here for several reasons: its default batch size and the synchronous API path it can fall back to for smaller files isn't built for this volume, it doesn't give you v2's automatic optimal chunking or clear visibility into per-batch failure isolation, and it's a desktop tool not well-suited to being the reliable, monitored, scheduled component of a nightly production integration — this calls for a proper Bulk API client (or an integration platform) with retry logic, failure alerting, and logging built in.
questions.professionalAnswer: Five million rows a night immediately rules out Data Loader as the actual integration mechanism — it's a great tool for a one-off cleanup, but it's not what I'd trust to run unattended every night with proper failure handling and alerting if something goes wrong at 2 AM. This needs to go through the Bulk API directly, ideally v2 so I'm not hand-tuning batch sizes. The decision I'd spend the most time on is parallel versus serial processing, because an ERP sync like this almost always has records that share a parent — multiple line items hitting the same order, multiple contacts hitting the same account — and parallel mode will happily try to update those related records in overlapping batches at the same time, which causes lock contention and failed batches that then have to retry, often costing more time than parallel mode saved. So my default assumption going in is serial mode, and I'd only move to parallel if I actually tested the data and confirmed there isn't that kind of relational overlap. And whatever client runs this needs real logging and alerting built in, because a silent partial failure on a 5-million-row nightly load is the kind of thing that doesn't get noticed until someone downstream asks why their numbers look wrong three days later.
commonMistakes: Recommends Data Loader as sufficient for a 5-million-row nightly production integration
Doesn't address parallel vs. serial mode or lock contention risk from shared parent records
Treats batch sizing as unimportant or ignores v1 vs. v2 differences
No mention of failure monitoring/alerting for an unattended nightly job

Explains the parallel vs. serial processing tradeoff and lock contention risk
Addresses batch sizing considerations (v1 manual sizing vs. v2 automatic chunking)
Addresses monitoring/alerting needs for an unattended nightly integration

questions.title: Permission Sets vs. Profiles as the Access Backbone for a 5,000-User Org
questions.prompt: An org with 5,000 users currently has 40 profiles, many nearly identical, each hand-built for a small variation in access. Explain the architectural case for shifting to a minimal-profile-plus-permission-sets model at this scale, and what actually has to be true for the migration to be safe.
questions.modelAnswer: Forty near-duplicate profiles at 5,000 users is a maintenance liability: profiles aren't efficiently assignable in combination (a user has exactly one profile), so any variation in access requires a new profile rather than composing access from reusable pieces, and keeping 40 profiles in sync as object or field-level security requirements evolve means the same change has to be replicated 40 times, with drift between them being almost inevitable over time. The architectural fix is to collapse down to a small number of baseline profiles representing genuinely distinct license types or fundamentally different UI/login requirements, and move everything else — the finer-grained variations in object, field, tab, or permission access — onto permission sets (and permission set groups, which bundle several permission sets as one assignable unit) layered on top. This is additive and composable: a user's effective access is the union of their profile plus every assigned permission set, so the same small set of permission sets can be mixed and matched instead of needing a new profile for every combination. For the migration to be safe, you need to do the access audit first: for every one of the 40 profiles, enumerate its actual effective permissions (not what it was originally intended to be, since profiles drift from their original design) and diff it against the others to find the genuine overlaps and the genuine, must-preserve differences. You then need a non-destructive cutover plan — build the new minimal profile plus permission set structure in a sandbox, assign it to a test cohort of real users from each old profile, and verify their effective access matches before touching production, because permission sets only ever add access, so any access a user is supposed to lose has to come out of their new baseline profile, not be assumed away.
questions.professionalAnswer: Forty profiles for 5,000 users with that much overlap is the kind of thing that looks fine until someone needs to change one field's visibility and realizes they have to make that change in twelve different places and hope they didn't miss one. The fix I'd pitch is: collapse down to a handful of base profiles that represent actual, meaningful differences — different license types, genuinely different UI — and push everything else onto permission sets, bundled into permission set groups where it makes sense, so access becomes something I compose rather than something I hand-build a new profile for every time. Permission sets only add access, never remove it, so the safety of the migration lives entirely in getting the new baseline profiles right — if someone's supposed to lose access they currently have, that has to come out of the profile they're moved to, not get assumed away because 'permission sets will handle it.' Before I touch production, I'd audit what each of the 40 profiles actually grants today, because profiles drift from their original intent over the years and I don't trust the original documentation to be accurate anymore. Then I'd build the new structure in a sandbox, move a real test cohort from each old profile over, and literally diff their effective access before and after, user by user, before I even think about a production cutover plan.

Proposes the migration without first auditing actual effective permissions on existing profiles
Assumes profiles can be collapsed arbitrarily without preserving genuine license/UI distinctions
No mention of a sandbox test cohort or before/after access verification before production cutover

Explains the additive, composable nature of permission sets/permission set groups
Requires an audit of actual effective permissions before migrating, not assumed documentation
Requires sandbox testing with a real user cohort and before/after verification before cutover

Correctly explains the additive permission set/profile model

questions.title: Restriction Rules and Scoping Rules vs. Sharing Rules: What Problem Do They Actually Solve
questions.prompt: Explain conceptually how Restriction Rules and Scoping Rules differ from sharing rules — specifically, whether they grant access or limit what's visible within access already granted — and give a scenario where you'd reach for one of them instead of redesigning the sharing model.
questions.modelAnswer: Sharing rules (and the rest of the standard sharing model — org-wide defaults, role hierarchy, manual sharing) are purely additive: they only ever grant more access than the baseline, never less. Restriction Rules invert that: they narrow what a user sees among records they already have access to, based on criteria, without changing the underlying sharing model at all — the use case is a user who, through role hierarchy or a broad sharing rule, technically has access to a wide set of records, but the business wants their default list views and search to surface only a relevant subset (for example, a regional rep who has org-wide read access to Accounts for reporting purposes, but whose day-to-day list views should default to only their region's Accounts) without actually taking away the broader access they need for the reporting use case. Scoping Rules solve a related but distinct problem specifically for list views and lookup/search results performance and relevance at scale, letting you set a default, narrower scope so users aren't paging through millions of technically-accessible records to find the ones relevant to their daily work. The key scenario where you reach for either instead of redesigning sharing: when the full access genuinely needs to remain in place for some purposes (reporting, escalation, cross-team collaboration) and the actual complaint is about UI clutter or irrelevant search results, not about unauthorized access — redesigning the sharing model in that case would be solving the wrong problem and likely breaking the legitimate broad-access use cases.
questions.professionalAnswer: The distinction I'd lead with is: sharing rules can only give you more, never less — if the complaint is 'this person can see things they shouldn't,' that's a sharing model problem, full stop. Restriction Rules are for the opposite complaint: the person's access is actually correct and needed — maybe they need org-wide Account visibility for a reporting role — but their everyday list views are drowning them in records outside their actual region, and the fix isn't to take away access they legitimately need, it's to narrow what shows up by default. Scoping Rules solve a cousin of that same problem specifically for list views and lookups at scale, so people aren't scrolling through a million technically-visible records to find the twenty that matter to their day. The scenario where I'd reach for one of these instead of touching the sharing model: someone comes to me saying search and list views are cluttered or slow, and when I dig in, their actual access is correct — they do need that broader visibility for some legitimate reason — so narrowing the sharing model would just break that reporting or escalation use case while not even really being what they're complaining about.
commonMistakes: Confuses Restriction/Scoping Rules with sharing rules as if they grant access
Doesn't explain that these narrow visibility within already-granted access, not security
Recommends redesigning the sharing model for a problem that's really about UI clutter/relevance
No concrete scenario distinguishing a true access problem from a visibility/relevance problem

Correctly explains Restriction/Scoping Rules as narrowing visibility within existing access, not a security mechanism
Distinguishes a genuine unauthorized-access problem from a UI relevance/clutter problem
Gives a concrete, correct scenario for reaching for one of these tools

Correctly explains what Restriction Rules and Scoping Rules actually do

questions.title: Designing Multi-Step Parallel Approval Processes That Don't Stall
questions.prompt: A quote approval process needs sign-off from both Legal and Finance in parallel before it can move to a final VP approval step, and the business wants the process to not stall indefinitely if one approver is out. What design decisions actually matter here?
questions.modelAnswer: Parallel approval steps let both Legal and Finance receive the approval request simultaneously rather than sequentially, which is the right structural choice here since neither approval logically depends on the other's outcome — sequencing them would simply add unnecessary latency. The design decisions that actually prevent stalling: first, decide and configure the step's completion rule correctly — 'require unanimous approval' means the step only completes once both approve, versus 'require only one approval' which completes as soon as either does, and the business requirement here (both sign off) means unanimous is correct, but that also means the step is exactly as slow as the slower of the two approvers, which is where the 'what if someone is out' risk actually lives. Second, configure a delegated approver for each approver in their user record (or an approval-process-level alternate), so an out-of-office Legal reviewer's request routes to a designated backup rather than sitting unactioned. Third, set a reasonable reminder/escalation mechanism — most orgs pair this with a scheduled flow or Apex job that checks for approval requests pending beyond a threshold and escalates or notifies a manager, since approval processes don't natively time out and auto-escalate on their own. Fourth, make sure the final VP approval step's entry criteria correctly requires both parallel approvals to have completed, not just one, which sounds obvious but is a common configuration mistake when parallel steps are set up.
questions.professionalAnswer: The structural piece is straightforward — Legal and Finance don't need to wait on each other, so this is a parallel step, not two sequential ones, and I'd configure it to require both approvals before moving on, since that's literally the requirement. The part that actually prevents stalling is less obvious: approval processes don't time out or escalate on their own, so if I don't configure a delegated approver on each approver's user record, an out-of-office Legal reviewer just means this sits untouched indefinitely with nobody even necessarily noticing. So every approver in this chain needs a designated backup configured, not just a polite Slack message asking someone to cover while they're out. I'd also want a scheduled check — a flow or a small Apex job — that flags any approval request that's been pending past a threshold, say 48 hours, and notifies a manager, because 'someone will probably notice' isn't a mechanism. And I'd double-check the VP step's entry criteria specifically requires both parallel approvals completed, not just one of them, because that's an easy misconfiguration that quietly lets an approval through with only half the required sign-off.
commonMistakes: Builds this as sequential approval steps instead of a parallel step
Doesn't configure delegated/alternate approvers to handle an out-of-office approver
Assumes approval processes auto-escalate on their own without a scheduled check
Doesn't verify the final step's entry criteria correctly requires both parallel approvals

Configures delegated/alternate approvers to prevent an out-of-office stall
Adds an explicit escalation/reminder mechanism since approvals don't auto-escalate
Verifies the downstream step's entry criteria correctly depends on both approvals

questions.title: Validation Rules vs. Flow Fault Handling: Where Each One Actually Belongs
questions.prompt: A data-quality requirement could be enforced either as a validation rule or as error-checking logic inside a record-triggered flow with a fault path. Explain the real tradeoffs between the two, and when you'd choose one over the other.
questions.modelAnswer: A validation rule runs synchronously at save time, before the record is committed, blocking the save entirely with a clear, user-facing error message attached to a specific field — it is the correct tool for a hard business rule that should never be allowed to exist in the data, regardless of which interface created the record (UI, API, data load, or another flow), because validation rules fire on every path into the object with no way to accidentally bypass them except explicit admin-level API flags. Flow fault-path handling, by contrast, exists to gracefully manage a failure within an automation's own logic — a DML operation inside the flow that fails for an unrelated reason (a different validation rule firing, a duplicate rule block, a lock contention error) — and route to a sensible fallback (notify someone, log the failure, roll back related changes cleanly) rather than let the flow fail with a cryptic, hard-to-read error. The key distinction: validation rules prevent bad data from ever being committed, full stop, on every save path; fault paths handle what happens when automation-driven DML unexpectedly fails, which is a different problem. A common mistake is putting a hard data-quality rule only inside a flow's logic (e.g., a Decision element checking a condition before allowing the flow to proceed) — that only catches the condition on the specific path that flow covers, and a record created via Data Loader, the API, or a different flow bypasses it entirely. I'd always put the non-negotiable data-quality rule in a validation rule, and reserve fault paths for genuinely unexpected automation failures, not for enforcing business rules.
questions.professionalAnswer: The question I'd ask first is: does this rule need to apply no matter how the record gets created — API, data load, another flow, anyone — or is this really about handling something going wrong inside this one specific automation? If it's the first, it has to be a validation rule, because that's the only mechanism that fires on every single path into the object, with basically no way around it short of an explicit bypass flag an admin would have to deliberately set. I've seen teams put a 'hard' business rule as a Decision element inside one flow and feel good about it, right up until someone loads data through the API or a different flow creates the record and the rule just... doesn't apply, because it was never actually enforced at the object level. Fault paths are solving a genuinely different problem — what happens when this flow's own DML unexpectedly fails, maybe because of lock contention or a different validation rule firing — and that's about failing gracefully, not about defining the business rule in the first place. So for this data-quality requirement specifically, I'm putting it in a validation rule, and I'd only add fault-path handling on top if the flow itself does DML that could fail for reasons unrelated to that rule.

Doesn't recognize that API/data-load/other-automation paths can bypass flow-only logic
Confuses fault-path handling with business-rule enforcement
Doesn't explain that validation rules run synchronously on every save path

Correctly explains what fault paths actually handle (unexpected DML failure, not business rules)

Gives a clear rule for choosing between the two

questions.title: Platform Events for Decoupled Automation Across Systems
questions.prompt: An order-fulfillment flow needs to notify an external warehouse system the moment an Opportunity closes, without making the Salesforce flow wait on that external system's response. Explain why a platform-event-triggered flow is a better architectural fit here than a direct outbound callout from the closing flow, and what you give up by decoupling it this way.
questions.modelAnswer: A direct synchronous callout from the closing flow ties the Opportunity-close transaction's success to the external warehouse system's availability and response time — if that system is slow or briefly down, the close operation itself is delayed or fails, which is the wrong coupling for a business event that should complete regardless of a downstream system's health. Publishing a platform event when the Opportunity closes decouples the two: the closing flow publishes the event and completes immediately, and a separate platform-event-triggered flow (or Apex trigger) subscribed to that event handles the actual outbound integration asynchronously, retrying independently of the original transaction if needed. This is the correct pattern specifically because the warehouse notification is not something the Opportunity-closing transaction needs to wait for or roll back on — it's a downstream side effect, not a dependency of the close itself. What you give up: strict ordering and immediacy guarantees (the subscriber processes the event on its own schedule, typically near-real-time but not instantaneous, and multiple events can be processed in a batch together, which changes how you think about per-event isolation), and debuggability becomes a two-step problem (you now have to trace both the publish and the separate subscribe/process steps rather than a single transaction's log), which means you need deliberate monitoring on both sides — confirming events are actually being published and confirming the subscriber is actually processing them — rather than relying on the simpler single-transaction failure visibility a direct callout would have given you.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I want to avoid is the Opportunity-close transaction's success depending on whether some warehouse system three integrations away happens to be responsive right now — that's exactly the kind of tight coupling that turns an unrelated outage into a Salesforce incident. So instead of a direct callout from the closing flow, I'd have that flow publish a platform event and be done — the close completes on its own, with zero dependency on the warehouse system's health. A separate flow or trigger subscribed to that event handles the actual outbound notification, and if the warehouse system is slow or down, that's a problem contained to the integration layer, not something blocking sales operations. What I'm giving up is the simplicity of one traceable transaction — now if something goes wrong, I'm checking two places: did the event actually publish, and did the subscriber actually process it? So I wouldn't ship this without some monitoring on both ends, because 'fire and forget' only works if someone's actually watching to confirm things are firing and getting forgotten correctly, not silently failing on either side.
commonMistakes: Recommends a direct synchronous callout and doesn't identify the coupling risk
Doesn't explain that platform events decouple publish from subscribe/process timing
Treats the decoupled approach as a free win with no tradeoffs
Doesn't mention needing monitoring on both the publish and subscribe sides
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the coupling risk of a direct synchronous callout
Correctly explains the publish/subscribe decoupling platform events provide
Identifies the tradeoff in ordering/immediacy guarantees and debuggability
Recommends monitoring on both sides of the decoupled flow

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies why direct callout coupling is the wrong fit
Correctly explains the platform event publish/subscribe mechanism
