questions.title: Building a Before-Save Flow for High-Volume Field Updates
questions.prompt: Walk through, step by step, how you'd build a before-save record-triggered flow on Opportunity that sets a Priority_Score__c formula-like calculation whenever Amount or CloseDate changes, including exactly which configuration choices make it a true before-save flow and not an after-save one.
questions.modelAnswer: Start the flow as a record-triggered flow on Opportunity, set to trigger the flow when a record is updated (and created, if new Opportunities also need the score), with entry conditions limited to 'Amount changed OR CloseDate changed' so the flow doesn't needlessly re-run on saves that don't affect the inputs to the calculation. The critical configuration choice is selecting 'Actions and Related Records' as 'No' for optimization when the flow's logic only needs to update fields on the triggering record itself — in Flow Builder this is the setting that keeps the flow in the before-save context, letting it update {!$Record.Priority_Score__c} directly in memory rather than performing a separate Update Records element, which would force it into an after-save context and trigger a second DML operation. Inside the flow, use an Assignment element (or a Decision plus multiple Assignments if the scoring logic branches) to set the field directly on $Record, with no Get Records, no Create/Update/Delete Records elements, and no actions that touch any other object — introducing any of those forces the flow out of before-save eligibility. Finally, test it by updating Amount on a handful of existing Opportunities and confirming the field updates with no visible second save in the record's field history (before-save updates to the same record don't generate a separate 'Last Modified' event the way an after-save Update Records element would).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd set this up as a record-triggered flow on Opportunity, triggered on create and update, with entry conditions scoped specifically to Amount or CloseDate changing — not just 'record updated' — so it's not doing unnecessary work on every unrelated save. The part I'd be careful about is keeping this a true before-save flow: that means the only element touching the record is a straight Assignment setting $Record.Priority_Score__c directly, no Get Records, no Update Records element, nothing reaching out to another object. The moment I add any of those, Flow pushes this into after-save territory and now I'm paying for a second DML operation I didn't need. Once it's built, I'd test it by updating Amount on a few real Opportunities and checking that the score updates without generating a separate field-history entry for a second save — that's my quick sanity check that I actually kept it in the cheap, before-save lane instead of accidentally building an after-save flow that happens to work.
commonMistakes: Adds an Update Records element, accidentally forcing the flow into after-save context
Sets entry conditions to 'record updated' generically instead of scoping to the relevant fields
Adds a Get Records call unnecessarily, which also forces after-save context
Doesn't verify afterward that the flow is actually running before-save
keyPoints: Scopes entry conditions to the specific fields that affect the calculation
Uses a direct Assignment on $Record instead of an Update Records element
Avoids any element (Get Records, Create/Update/Delete, other-object actions) that forces after-save context
Verifies the flow is actually running before-save after building it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly configures entry conditions scoped to the relevant fields
Correctly keeps the flow in before-save context (Assignment on $Record only)
Avoids elements that would force after-save context
Verifies the result after building

questions.title: Bulkifying a Flow That Updates Related Child Records in a Loop
questions.prompt: You inherit a flow that, for every Account updated, loops through its Contacts and updates each one's Mailing_Status__c individually inside the loop using a per-iteration Update Records element. It works fine on single-record saves but times out on a 5,000-record batch update. Walk through exactly how you'd rebuild the loop to be properly bulkified.
questions.modelAnswer: The root problem is an Update Records element placed inside the loop, which issues one DML statement per Contact per Account rather than one bulk DML statement for the whole set — Flow does not automatically defer and batch DML calls that are explicitly placed inside a loop, so this pattern multiplies both DML statement count and total execution time linearly with record count, which is exactly why it survives single-record testing and collapses at 5,000 records with their associated Contacts. The fix: inside the loop, use an Assignment element to add each updated Contact (with its Mailing_Status__c field set) to a collection variable, performing no DML inside the loop at all — only building up the collection in memory. After the loop completes, place a single Update Records element outside the loop that updates the entire collection variable in one DML call. This converts what was N DML operations into exactly one, and Flow's own bulkification of that single Update Records call across the whole triggering transaction's set of Accounts then works correctly, since the expensive operation is no longer repeated per iteration. I'd test this by running the same 5,000-record batch update again and confirming via debug/trace that only one DML statement fires for the Contact updates, not thousands.
questions.professionalAnswer: The giveaway here is an Update Records element sitting inside the loop — that's going to fire once per Contact, every single time, and Flow doesn't quietly batch that up for you just because it's inside a loop. It'll look completely fine on a one-record test because one Account's Contacts is a handful of DML calls, and then it falls over on a 5,000-record batch because now it's potentially tens of thousands of individual updates. The fix is always the same shape: nothing that writes to the database goes inside the loop. Inside the loop, I'm just using an Assignment to add each Contact, with its field already set, into a collection variable — pure in-memory work, no DML. Then after the loop finishes, one single Update Records element updates that whole collection in one shot. That's it — same outcome, but now it's one DML operation instead of thousands. Before I call it done, I'd actually rerun the 5,000-record batch and check the debug logs to confirm I'm seeing one update call, not a pile of them, because I don't want to just assume the fix worked.
commonMistakes: Doesn't identify the Update Records element inside the loop as the actual root cause
Moves the DML outside the loop but forgets to build a collection variable first
Assumes testing on a single record is sufficient to confirm the fix
Doesn't verify via debug/trace that only one DML call fires after the fix
keyPoints: Correctly identifies DML inside the loop as the root cause of the timeout
Builds a collection variable inside the loop with no DML
Moves the single Update Records element outside the loop, after it completes
Verifies the fix with a realistic batch-size test and debug/trace

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses DML-inside-loop as the root cause
Correctly rebuilds using a collection variable with no DML in the loop
Correctly moves the single DML operation outside the loop
Verifies the fix with an appropriately-sized test

questions.title: Designing a Reusable Subflow for Address Validation
questions.prompt: Three different flows (Lead conversion, Account update, and a Contact screen flow) each need to validate and standardize a mailing address the same way. Walk through how you'd design this as a single reusable subflow, including what inputs and outputs it needs and how you'd avoid it becoming a hidden single point of failure.
questions.modelAnswer: Build a single autolaunched flow dedicated to address validation/standardization, defined with explicit input variables (the raw address fields: street, city, state, postal code, country) marked as Available for Input, and explicit output variables (the standardized versions of those same fields, plus a boolean or status output indicating whether validation succeeded or what, if anything, was corrected) marked as Available for Output. Each of the three calling flows then adds a Subflow element, maps its own local address fields to the subflow's inputs, and maps the subflow's outputs back to its own variables, rather than three separate flows each re-implementing the same standardization logic independently and inevitably drifting apart over time. To avoid this becoming a hidden single point of failure: give the subflow its own explicit fault path so a failure inside address validation (an API callout to a validation service timing out, for instance) doesn't crash all three calling flows with an unhelpful error — instead it should return a clear 'validation failed, raw address passed through unchanged' output the caller can act on deliberately. Also version and test the subflow independently with its own test coverage before changes to it ship, since a change intended to fix one caller's edge case can silently break the other two if they're not all considered together — document which flows call this subflow directly in its description field so that's discoverable, not something you have to search metadata to find.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this once, as its own autolaunched flow, with clearly named input variables for the raw address fields and output variables for the standardized versions plus a status flag saying whether anything actually got corrected or validation failed outright. All three calling flows just drop in a Subflow element, map their fields in, map the results back out, and that's the entire integration point — no copy-pasted logic sitting in three places quietly drifting apart as someone tweaks one copy and forgets the other two. The single-point-of-failure risk is real though, so I'd make sure the subflow has its own fault path that returns a clean 'didn't validate, here's the original address' result instead of letting some callout timeout blow up all three parent flows with a generic error. And since three different flows now depend on this one subflow, I'm not changing it casually — any update gets tested against all three callers' actual use cases, and I'd put a note right in the subflow's description listing which flows call it, so six months from now whoever touches it knows exactly what they might break.
commonMistakes: Builds the validation logic three separate times instead of as one reusable subflow
Doesn't define explicit input/output variables, relying on implicit global variable sharing
No fault-path handling specific to the subflow, letting a failure propagate as a generic crash
Doesn't document which flows depend on the subflow, making future changes risky
keyPoints: Builds one autolaunched subflow with explicit input/output variables
Has all three calling flows map inputs/outputs through a Subflow element
Gives the subflow its own fault path with a graceful degraded output
Documents and tests against all dependent callers before changing the subflow

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the subflow with explicit input/output variables
Correctly wires all three callers through a Subflow element
Addresses fault handling to avoid a hidden single point of failure
Addresses documentation/testing discipline for a shared dependency

questions.title: Adding Fault Handling to a Flow That Currently Fails Silently
questions.prompt: A screen flow that creates a Case and two related Tasks has no fault paths configured anywhere, and when the Task creation occasionally fails due to a validation rule, the user sees a generic error screen with no useful information, and the Case is left created with no Tasks. Walk through exactly how you'd rebuild this with proper fault handling.
questions.modelAnswer: Every element in the flow that performs DML (the Create Records element for the Case, and the Create Records element for the two Tasks) needs its own explicit fault connector configured, rather than leaving Flow's default unhandled-fault behavior, which just surfaces a generic, unhelpful error screen to the user and leaves the transaction in whatever partial state it reached. For the Task creation step specifically, the fault path should route to a Screen element that displays the actual fault message (using {!$Flow.FaultMessage} merge field) in a user-readable way, telling the user specifically that the Case was created but the Tasks were not, rather than a generic failure. More importantly, this surfaces a transactional design question: if Tasks failing to create should mean the whole operation is considered incomplete, the flow needs to be restructured so the Case and Task creation happen in a way that can be rolled back together, or the user needs an explicit retry path for just the Task creation step rather than being told to start over and risk creating a duplicate Case. A clean design: create the Case first, then attempt Task creation with its own fault path that, on failure, shows the user the specific validation error and a button to retry just the Task creation against the already-created Case ID, rather than forcing a full restart that duplicates the Case.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I'd do is put an explicit fault path on both Create Records elements — right now, with no fault connector configured, Flow's own generic error screen is all the user ever sees, and it tells them nothing and leaves the Case half-created with no Tasks, which is worse than useful. I'd route the Task creation's fault path to a screen that actually shows {!$Flow.FaultMessage} in plain language, so the user and I both know exactly what validation rule tripped. But the real design fix here is bigger than just catching the error — right now a user who hits this gets told to 'try again,' which creates a second, duplicate Case, because the flow has no concept of resuming from where it failed. So I'd restructure this so Task creation's fault path offers a retry specifically against the Case that already got created, using its record ID, instead of restarting the whole flow from scratch. That's the difference between technically catching the error and actually giving the user a path that doesn't make the problem worse.
commonMistakes: Only adds a generic fault screen without surfacing the actual fault message
Doesn't address the partial-completion problem (Case created, Tasks not)
Lets a retry restart the whole flow, risking a duplicate Case
Leaves DML elements with no fault connector configured at all
keyPoints: Adds explicit fault connectors on every DML element, not just a generic catch-all
Surfaces the actual fault message to the user in a readable way
Addresses the partial-completion/transactional design problem, not just the error display
Designs a retry path that doesn't risk duplicating the already-created Case

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Adds explicit, element-specific fault handling
Surfaces a useful, specific error message to the user
Correctly identifies and addresses the partial-completion design problem
Designs a safe retry path avoiding duplicate record creation

questions.title: Debugging a Flow That Passes in Testing but Fails for Real Users
questions.prompt: A record-triggered flow passes every manual test you run as a System Administrator, but regular sales reps report it silently doesn't run at all. Walk through the specific debugging steps you'd take, in order, to find the actual cause.
questions.modelAnswer: First, check whether the flow is set to run in system context without sharing, with user context, or in the user's own context with field-level security enforced — a very common cause of exactly this symptom is a flow that checks or updates a field the sales rep's profile or permission sets don't have field-level access to, which fails silently or partially for a standard user but works fine for a System Administrator profile, which typically has access to everything. Second, check the entry conditions and any Decision element logic against the actual data a sales rep's records would have versus the data used in admin testing — if the admin tested with records they themselves own or with fuller data, but reps' records look different (missing a field, different record type), the flow may correctly not be entering for reps' actual data and 'not running' may actually be correct behavior given different entry criteria. Third, use the flow's own debug/run tool but explicitly run it as or impersonate a rep user (via Login As, if available, or by checking the audit trail / debug logs filtered to that rep's user) rather than testing only as yourself, since Flow Builder's 'Debug' feature run as an admin will not surface permission-based failures a rep would actually hit. Fourth, check whether the flow references a formula, Apex action, or object the rep's profile doesn't have access to at all, which can cause the flow to fail or skip silently rather than throwing a visible error for a lower-privileged user.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first assumption, honestly, is a permissions gap, because 'works for me, silently doesn't for reps' is the classic signature of field-level security or object access that my admin profile just doesn't hit. So first I'd check whether the flow runs in system context or user context, and if it's user context, I'd check field-level security and CRUD on every field and object this flow touches against the actual sales rep profile, not mine. Second, I'd pull a real rep's record that's supposedly not triggering the flow and walk it through the entry conditions by hand, because it's entirely possible the flow is correctly not entering — reps' data might just look different from what I tested with. Third, I would not trust my own Debug run in Flow Builder as proof this works for reps, because running Debug as myself tests my own permissions, not theirs — I'd use Login As to actually become a rep and trigger the real scenario, or pull debug logs filtered to that user if Login As isn't available. And I'd specifically check whether any field, object, or Apex action the flow touches is something the rep's profile simply can't see — that's usually where this kind of silent, admin-invisible failure is actually hiding.
commonMistakes: Only retests as an admin instead of impersonating or checking logs for the actual affected user
Doesn't check field-level security/object permissions differences between admin and rep profiles
Assumes the flow is broken without first confirming entry conditions against real rep data
Doesn't check whether the flow runs in system vs. user context
keyPoints: Checks the flow's running context (system vs. user) as a first diagnostic step
Checks field-level security/object permissions specific to the rep's actual profile
Verifies entry conditions against real rep data rather than assuming the flow is broken
Tests as or impersonating the actual affected user rather than relying on admin-context debug runs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies running context (system vs. user) as a key diagnostic
Correctly investigates field-level security/permissions gap
Verifies entry conditions against real affected-user data before assuming a bug
Uses an appropriate method to test as the actual affected user

questions.title: Configuring Parallel Approval Steps in an Approval Process
questions.prompt: Walk through, step by step, how you'd configure an approval process so that Legal and Finance both receive and must both complete an approval step in parallel, before a final VP step, including the specific settings that make it parallel rather than sequential.
questions.modelAnswer: In Setup, create the approval process on the relevant object (Quote), define entry criteria, then build the first approval step. Within that step, when assigning approvers, choose 'Automatically assign to approver(s)' and add both the Legal and Finance approvers (or their queues/roles) to the same step rather than creating two separate sequential steps. Critically, set the step's approver response requirement to 'Approve if ALL approvers approve' (unanimous), which is what actually makes the two responses parallel and jointly required, rather than 'Approve if ANY approver approves,' which would let either one alone complete the step. Configure email/notification templates so both Legal and Finance are notified simultaneously when the request enters this step, not sequentially. Then create a second approval step for the VP, with entry criteria on this step correctly scoped to trigger only once the first (parallel) step has fully completed with approval from both parties, not on simple record submission. Finally, configure rejection behavior explicitly: decide whether a rejection from either Legal or Finance immediately kills the whole process (typical for a unanimous-requirement step) or routes to a defined rejection path, and test the full scenario by submitting a record and having each approver act independently, confirming the VP step only becomes active after both complete.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this as one approval step containing both approvers, not two sequential steps — that's the part that actually makes it parallel. When I assign approvers to that step, I add both Legal and Finance to the same step, and then the setting I'd double check most carefully is the response requirement: it needs to be set to require approval from all assigned approvers, not just one, because 'any one approver' would let this slip through with only Finance's sign-off and no Legal review at all, which defeats the whole point. Notifications go out to both at the same time since they're in the same step. Then the VP step comes after, and I'd verify its entry criteria actually depends on that first step being fully, successfully completed — not just on the record being submitted — because I've seen approval processes misconfigured so the final step fires too early. Before I'd consider this done, I'd actually submit a test record and have both approvers act on it separately, confirming the VP step doesn't light up until both of them are in, and I'd also nail down what happens if either one rejects, because that needs to be an explicit decision, not an assumption.
commonMistakes: Builds Legal and Finance as two sequential steps instead of one parallel step
Sets the approver response requirement to 'any' instead of 'all', breaking the parallel requirement
Doesn't verify the VP step's entry criteria depends on full completion of the parallel step
Doesn't explicitly define or test rejection behavior
keyPoints: Correctly configures both approvers within a single step, not sequential steps
Correctly sets the unanimous ('all approvers') response requirement
Verifies the downstream VP step's entry criteria depends on full parallel-step completion
Explicitly configures and tests rejection behavior

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly configures a single parallel step with both approvers
Correctly sets the unanimous approval requirement
Correctly scopes the downstream step's entry criteria
Addresses and tests rejection behavior

questions.title: Configuring Role Hierarchy and Sharing Rules for a Service Organization
questions.prompt: A support organization has Tier 1, Tier 2, and Tier 3 agents, plus team leads who need to see their whole team's Cases, and Tier 3 specialists who need to see escalated Cases regardless of which team they came from. Walk through the actual role hierarchy and sharing rule configuration you'd build.
questions.modelAnswer: Set the organization-wide default for Case to Private (or Public Read Only, depending on broader reporting needs), since the requirement is clearly that access needs to be actively granted, not open by default. Build the role hierarchy with each Tier 1/Tier 2 team's agents reporting up to their team lead's role, which automatically grants each team lead visibility into their own team's Cases through standard role-hierarchy access — no additional sharing rule needed for that specific requirement. For Tier 3 specialists needing escalated Cases regardless of originating team, role hierarchy alone won't work since those agents don't sit above every team in the hierarchy; instead, create a criteria-based sharing rule on Case: 'where Escalation_Level__c equals Tier 3' (or a similar status/flag field marking a Case as escalated), shared with the Tier 3 public group, granting Read/Write access. This is the correct mechanism because it's the Case's own attribute (escalated or not) that determines visibility, not the viewer's position in a team hierarchy. I'd also set up a public group containing all Tier 3 specialists rather than referencing a role directly in the sharing rule, since public groups are more flexible to maintain as the specialist roster changes. Finally, I'd test with a sample Tier 1 agent, a team lead, and a Tier 3 specialist logged in separately (or via Login As) to confirm each sees exactly the Cases they should and no more.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start with Case locked down to Private org-wide, since the whole point here is that access needs to be deliberate. For the team lead requirement, I don't need a sharing rule at all — if I build the role hierarchy so each team's agents report up to their lead's role, the lead automatically sees their team's Cases through standard hierarchy access, that's free. The Tier 3 piece is different because it's not about team structure, it's about a Case's own status — an escalated Case needs to be visible to Tier 3 regardless of which team it came from, and role hierarchy can't express that. So that's a criteria-based sharing rule: any Case flagged as Tier 3 escalated gets shared with a Tier 3 public group. I'd use a public group rather than pointing the rule at a role directly, because specialist rosters change and a group is much easier to maintain than editing the rule itself every time someone joins or leaves that team. Before I'd call this done, I'd actually log in as a sample agent from each tier — or use Login As — and confirm each one sees exactly what they should, because sharing model changes are exactly the kind of thing where 'I'm pretty sure this is right' isn't good enough.
commonMistakes: Tries to solve the Tier 3 escalation requirement with role hierarchy instead of a criteria-based sharing rule
Doesn't recognize team lead visibility is already covered by role hierarchy with no extra sharing rule needed
References a role directly in the sharing rule instead of a more maintainable public group
Doesn't test the configuration from each affected user's actual perspective
keyPoints: Correctly sets org-wide default to Private given the access requirements
Correctly uses role hierarchy alone for team lead visibility, with no redundant sharing rule
Correctly uses a criteria-based sharing rule for the Tier 3 escalation requirement
Uses a public group for maintainability and tests from each affected user's perspective

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly sets org-wide defaults and uses role hierarchy for team lead visibility
Correctly designs the criteria-based sharing rule for Tier 3 escalation
Uses a public group appropriately for maintainability
Tests the configuration from each affected user's perspective

questions.title: Setting Up Case Teams and Queues for Dynamic Routing
questions.prompt: A support process needs incoming Cases to land in a queue by product line, then have specific additional people (an account manager, sometimes a specialist) added to just that one Case without changing anyone's broader access. Walk through the actual configuration.
questions.modelAnswer: Create one queue per product line, with membership set to the agents who support that product, and use an assignment rule (or a flow, if routing logic is more complex than simple criteria) that evaluates the incoming Case's product field and reassigns ownership to the matching queue, which immediately grants every queue member access to that Case without any additional sharing configuration since queue ownership itself grants access to members. For the per-Case addition of an account manager or specialist, Case Teams are the correct tool rather than modifying sharing rules or public groups: enable Case Teams on the object if not already active, define Case Team Roles (e.g., 'Account Manager', 'Technical Specialist') with the access level each role should have, and add specific individuals to a specific Case's team as needed — this grants access scoped to that one Case only, with no broader change to the account manager's general visibility into other Cases. For repeat scenarios (the same account manager needing to be added to every Case for their accounts), set up Default Case Teams on the Account so the relevant people are automatically added to every new Case under that account, removing the need for manual addition each time. I'd test this by creating a sample Case for each product line, confirming it routes to the right queue, then manually adding a team member and confirming their access is scoped to that Case alone.
questions.professionalAnswer: The queue piece is pretty mechanical — one queue per product line, membership set to whoever supports that product, and an assignment rule that reads the incoming Case's product field and routes it to the right queue. Once it's queue-owned, every member of that queue already has access, no extra sharing rule needed. The more interesting part is the 'add one specific person to one specific Case' requirement, and that's exactly what Case Teams are for, not sharing rules or public groups — I'd define Case Team Roles like Account Manager and Technical Specialist with whatever access level each needs, and then people get added to an individual Case's team as needed, which only grants them access to that one Case, nothing else that account manager might be tangentially connected to. If this is actually a recurring pattern — the same account manager needs to be on every Case for their accounts — I wouldn't make someone do that by hand every time; I'd set up Default Case Teams on the Account so they're added automatically the moment a new Case is created under it. I'd test the whole thing end to end — a Case per product line routing correctly, then a manual team addition confirmed to be scoped to just that Case.
commonMistakes: Uses a public group or sharing rule to add one person to one Case instead of Case Teams
Doesn't recognize queue ownership already grants access to queue members with no extra rule needed
Doesn't propose Default Case Teams for a recurring per-account pattern
Doesn't verify Case Team access is actually scoped to the single Case, not broader
keyPoints: Correctly configures queues per product line with an assignment mechanism
Correctly uses Case Teams and Case Team Roles for per-Case, scoped access
Recommends Default Case Teams for recurring per-account patterns
Verifies routing and scoped access through actual testing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly configures queues and routing by product line
Correctly uses Case Teams for scoped, per-Case access
Recommends Default Case Teams for the recurring pattern
Verifies the configuration with concrete testing

questions.title: Upserting 2 Million Child Records with External IDs During a Migration
questions.prompt: You need to load 2 million Contact records from a legacy system into Salesforce, each needing to link to the correct Account by the legacy system's account number, which doesn't exist as a Salesforce field yet. Walk through exactly how you'd configure this load.
questions.modelAnswer: First, create a custom field on Account, Legacy_Account_Number__c, and mark it as an External ID (and ideally also Unique) so Salesforce can use it as a lookup key during the load rather than requiring the actual Salesforce Account ID, which the legacy system doesn't know. Load or update Accounts first with that external ID populated, confirming every Account that needs to receive Contacts already has its Legacy_Account_Number__c set correctly — this has to complete and be verified before the Contact load runs, since the Contact load depends on being able to resolve this relationship. For the Contact load itself, use the Bulk API (via Data Loader's bulk mode or a direct Bulk API client, appropriate given the 2 million row volume) with an upsert operation, mapping the Contact's AccountId lookup field to the Account's Legacy_Account_Number__c external ID field rather than to Account ID directly — Data Loader's field mapping supports mapping a lookup to an external ID field specifically for this purpose, and Salesforce resolves the relationship by matching values during the load rather than requiring you to pre-fetch and map actual Salesforce IDs yourself. Before running the full 2 million rows, I'd run a small test batch (a few hundred records spanning a range of Account relationships, including some edge cases like a legacy account number with no matching Account) to confirm the mapping resolves correctly and to see what the error behavior looks like for unmatched values, then run the full load with serial or parallel mode chosen based on whether records share parent Accounts heavily (serial if so, to avoid lock contention).
questions.professionalAnswer: The key piece here is getting a real External ID field onto Account before touching Contacts at all — I'd add a custom field, Legacy Account Number, mark it as an External ID and unique, and make sure every Account that should receive Contacts already has that value populated and verified. That's a hard prerequisite; I'm not starting the Contact load until I've confirmed that. Then for the actual Contact load, at 2 million rows this is Bulk API territory, not a casual Data Loader run with default settings. The trick that makes the relationship work without needing actual Salesforce Account IDs is mapping the Contact's Account lookup field directly to that external ID field during the load — Salesforce does the matching for me. But I wouldn't run all 2 million rows on faith; I'd do a test batch first, including some records with account numbers that deliberately don't match anything, just to see exactly how the load behaves on a miss before it's happening at scale. And depending on whether a lot of these Contacts share parent Accounts, I'd lean toward serial processing mode to avoid lock contention from a lot of concurrent updates hitting the same Account.
commonMistakes: Tries to map the Contact's Account lookup to the actual Salesforce Account ID instead of an external ID
Doesn't create and populate the external ID field on Account before starting the Contact load
Skips a small test batch before running the full 2-million-row load
Doesn't consider parallel vs. serial mode given shared-parent relationship risk
keyPoints: Creates and populates an External ID field on Account before the Contact load
Maps the Contact's lookup field to the external ID during the upsert, not to Account ID
Runs a test batch first, including deliberately unmatched values
Chooses processing mode appropriately given the relationship structure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly sets up and sequences the External ID field on Account
Correctly maps the lookup via external ID during the Contact upsert
Runs a sensible test batch before the full load
Addresses Bulk API processing mode appropriately for the scale

questions.title: Configuring Matching and Duplicate Rules for Lead/Contact Dedup
questions.prompt: Marketing complains that the same person is showing up as both a Lead and an existing Contact repeatedly, and reps are wasting time working Leads that are actually the same person. Walk through the actual Matching Rule and Duplicate Rule configuration you'd build.
questions.modelAnswer: Build a custom Matching Rule across Lead and Contact comparing Email using an exact match algorithm (email is the most reliable identity signal available) and, as a secondary matching criterion, Last Name plus a fuzzy match on First Name combined with an exact or fuzzy match on company/account name, since relying on email alone will miss legitimate duplicates entered with a different or personal email address. Activate this matching rule, then build a Duplicate Rule referencing it, configured specifically for the Lead object comparing against existing Contacts (and existing Leads, to catch duplicate Lead entry too) — set the duplicate rule action to 'Alert' with a clear, actionable message rather than 'Block', at least initially, since blocking outright risks preventing legitimate new Lead creation on an imperfect match and frustrates reps if false positives occur; the alert should show the matched existing record directly in the UI so a rep can immediately see and act on it rather than just being told a duplicate might exist. I'd also configure the duplicate rule to run on both create and edit so existing bad data entering a transition doesn't get missed. After rollout, I'd monitor the actual match rate for a couple of weeks — checking how often reps dismiss the alert versus act on it — before considering tightening the action to a stricter block in scenarios where the match confidence is consistently high (e.g., exact email match specifically), since that data tells you whether the matching rule's precision justifies a harder block.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start the matching rule with email as the primary signal — exact match, since that's the most reliable way to tell two records are the same person — but I wouldn't stop there, because plenty of real duplicates come in with a different email address, so I'd add a secondary match on last name plus a fuzzy match on first name and company. Once that matching rule's built and activated, the duplicate rule sits on top of it, comparing incoming Leads against both existing Contacts and existing Leads. For the action, I'd start with Alert, not Block — showing the rep the matched record right there in the UI so they can see it and decide, rather than hard-blocking Lead creation on what might occasionally be a false positive and just annoying reps into finding workarounds. I'd run it on both create and edit, not just create, so I'm not missing duplicates introduced later. And I wouldn't just set this and walk away — I'd actually watch how reps respond to the alerts for a couple of weeks, and if the exact-email matches are consistently correct with basically no false positives, that's when I'd consider tightening that specific scenario to an actual block instead of just an alert.
commonMistakes: Relies on email as the only matching criterion, missing duplicates with different emails
Sets the duplicate rule action to Block immediately without first measuring false-positive rate
Doesn't check against both existing Leads and existing Contacts
Doesn't configure the rule to also run on edit, missing duplicates introduced later
keyPoints: Builds a matching rule with email plus a secondary fuzzy-match signal
Compares against both existing Contacts and existing Leads
Starts with an Alert action, showing the matched record, rather than an immediate Block
Monitors real-world match behavior before tightening to a stricter action

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the matching rule with appropriate primary/secondary signals
Correctly scopes the duplicate rule against both Leads and Contacts
Chooses an appropriate initial action (Alert vs. Block) with reasoning
Proposes monitoring before tightening the rule

questions.title: Data Loader Practice Lab, At Production Scale: Mass Updating Related Records Safely
questions.prompt: You need to mass-update the Owner field on 150,000 Opportunities to redistribute them across a restructured sales team, while preserving the existing Stage and Amount values untouched. Walk through the actual Data Loader (or Bulk API) steps you'd take, and the safety checks you'd run before and after.
questions.modelAnswer: First, export the current state of all 150,000 Opportunities (Id, current OwnerId, Stage, Amount, and any other fields that matter for verification) as a backup/reference file before making any change, since a mass ownership change is straightforward to reverse only if you have the prior state recorded. Build the update file with just two columns populated for the update operation: Id and the new OwnerId, resolved via whatever business logic maps old owners/territories to new owners (this mapping should be validated by the business before the load, not assumed). Use Data Loader's Update operation (not Upsert, since every record already exists and you want to guard against accidentally creating new records on a typo) pointed only at Id and OwnerId columns — critically, don't include Stage or Amount in the mapped columns at all, since an Update operation only touches the fields actually included in the mapping, leaving every other field untouched; this is the mechanism that protects Stage and Amount automatically, not something that needs separate protection logic. Given the volume, use Bulk API mode, and check whether the new owners share territories in a way that would create lock contention (likely minimal here since it's just an owner field, but still worth considering in serial vs. parallel mode choice). After the load, spot-check a sample of updated records comparing against the pre-change export to confirm OwnerId changed as expected and Stage/Amount are unchanged, and run a report grouping by new Owner to confirm the overall distribution matches what the business intended.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I touch anything, I'm exporting every one of those 150,000 Opportunities as they currently stand — Id, current owner, Stage, Amount — because if this goes wrong in any way, that export is the only clean way back. For the actual update, I only map two columns: Id and the new OwnerId. I'd deliberately use Update, not Upsert, because Upsert on a typo'd or missing Id risks silently creating a brand new Opportunity instead of updating an existing one, and that's not a mistake I want available as an option here. The reassuring part is that Stage and Amount don't need separate protection — an Update operation only touches columns actually included in the mapping, so if they're not in my file, Data Loader doesn't touch them at all. At 150,000 rows I'd run this through Bulk API rather than Data Loader's default smaller-batch mode. Once it's done, I don't just trust the success count — I'd spot-check a sample against my original export to confirm owners actually changed and Stage/Amount didn't move, and I'd run a quick report grouped by new owner to sanity-check the redistribution actually matches what the business asked for.
commonMistakes: Uses Upsert instead of Update, risking accidental record creation on a bad Id
Doesn't export a pre-change backup before running the update
Includes Stage/Amount in the mapping unnecessarily out of caution instead of understanding Update's field-level behavior
Doesn't verify the result against the backup or with a distribution report afterward
keyPoints: Exports a pre-change backup before running the mass update
Uses Update (not Upsert) with only Id and OwnerId mapped
Correctly understands that Update only touches mapped fields, protecting Stage/Amount
Verifies the result with spot checks and a distribution report after the load

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Takes a pre-change backup/export as a safety step
Correctly uses Update rather than Upsert, with minimal field mapping
Correctly explains why Stage/Amount are protected by the mapping itself
Verifies results after the load with concrete checks

questions.title: Configuring Dynamic Forms for Conditional Field Visibility by Record Type
questions.prompt: A custom app's Opportunity page needs to show a completely different set of fields depending on whether the Opportunity's Record Type is 'New Business' versus 'Renewal', without maintaining two separate page layouts that drift out of sync. Walk through how you'd build this with Dynamic Forms.
questions.modelAnswer: Convert the Opportunity page layout to Dynamic Forms (if not already migrated), which moves fields off the static page layout and onto the Lightning page itself as individually placed field components, each with its own visibility filters, rather than requiring two entirely separate page layouts assigned by record type. On the Lightning Record Page, add the fields relevant to both record types as individual Field components inside a Field Section (or multiple sections), and for the fields specific to only one record type, set a Component Visibility filter on that field component based on {!Record.RecordType.Name} (or the RecordTypeId) equals 'New Business' or 'Renewal' as appropriate — this way the same single Lightning page serves both record types, showing and hiding fields dynamically rather than maintaining divergent static layouts. For fields common to both record types, place them with no visibility filter so they always show. I'd organize the page with a 'Common Fields' section with no filters at the top, followed by a 'New Business Fields' section and a 'Renewal Fields' section, each with a section-level or field-level visibility filter tied to Record Type, which also keeps the page itself easy for another admin to read and understand later. Finally, activate the page as the default for the Opportunity object (or assign it per app/profile as needed) and test by creating or viewing a sample Opportunity of each record type to confirm the right fields show and no unrelated fields leak through.
questions.professionalAnswer: The whole point of Dynamic Forms here is that I don't want to maintain two page layouts that are 90% the same and will inevitably drift apart the first time someone updates one and forgets the other. So I'd move Opportunity onto Dynamic Forms if it isn't already, then build this as one Lightning page with individual field components, not two layouts. Fields both record types need go in with no visibility filter — they just always show. Fields specific to New Business or Renewal get a Component Visibility filter checking the Record Type field, so the same page quietly shows or hides the right fields depending on what you're looking at. I'd actually organize it into labeled sections — common fields, then New Business fields, then Renewal fields — partly for the end user, but honestly also so the next admin who opens this page in Lightning App Builder can immediately see the structure instead of having to click through every field's visibility rule to figure out what's going on. Before I'd call it done, I'd pull up one Opportunity of each record type and confirm exactly the right fields show, nothing extra leaking through from the other type.
commonMistakes: Builds two separate page layouts instead of using Dynamic Forms' per-field visibility filters
Doesn't use Component Visibility filters tied to Record Type, instead building separate pages per record type
Doesn't organize the page clearly enough for future admins to understand the visibility logic
Doesn't test both record types' actual rendered page before considering it done
keyPoints: Correctly uses Dynamic Forms with per-field Component Visibility filters instead of duplicate layouts
Filters based on Record Type to show/hide the right fields
Organizes the page into clear sections for maintainability
Tests both record types' rendered result before finishing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses Dynamic Forms instead of duplicate page layouts
Correctly configures Component Visibility filters based on Record Type
Organizes the page for maintainability
Tests both record type scenarios before finishing

questions.title: Designing a Roll-Up Summary Through a Junction Object
questions.prompt: A custom app needs to show, on a Project record, the total hours logged across all Team Members assigned to it — but Team Member is a junction object between Project and Employee, and a standard roll-up summary field only works on a direct master-detail child. Walk through how you'd actually get this number onto the Project record.
questions.modelAnswer: A standard Roll-Up Summary field requires a direct master-detail relationship between the parent and the object being summed, so if the Team Member junction object has a master-detail relationship to Project (which it should, as the junction object genuinely belongs to the Project), the roll-up summary needs to sum a field on Team Member itself, not on Employee — so the actual fix is to have a Hours_Logged__c field living on the Team Member junction record itself (populated by whatever process logs hours against that specific assignment), and the Roll-Up Summary field on Project sums Team Member's Hours_Logged__c directly, since Team Member is the direct master-detail child, which satisfies the requirement without needing to reach through to Employee at all. If hours are actually logged against Employee directly rather than against the specific Project assignment, and Employee has no direct master-detail relationship to Project (which it shouldn't, since an Employee can work on many Projects), a standard Roll-Up Summary can't reach through that indirect relationship — the correct fix there is a Flow or Apex trigger on Employee's hour-logging records that updates a running total on the relevant Team Member junction record, which then correctly roll-up-summarizes onto Project through the direct master-detail relationship, keeping the chain of direct relationships intact at each step rather than trying to skip a level.
questions.professionalAnswer: The constraint I'd explain first is that a Roll-Up Summary field only works one level deep, through an actual master-detail relationship — and Team Member should already be master-detail to Project, since it's a junction record that only makes sense in the context of a specific Project. So the real question is: does the hours number live on Team Member itself, or does it live further away on Employee? If it's already a field on Team Member — Hours Logged for this specific assignment — this is easy, I just build the Roll-Up Summary on Project summing that field directly, done. If hours are actually being logged somewhere on Employee's side instead, that's a problem, because Employee isn't master-detail to Project — it can't be, since one Employee works on many Projects — so a Roll-Up Summary can't reach through that chain. In that case I'd build a small piece of automation, a flow or trigger, that takes whatever's being logged on the Employee side and rolls it up one level onto the Team Member junction record first, and then the existing Roll-Up Summary on Project picks it up automatically because Team Member is the direct child it was always designed to summarize.
commonMistakes: Tries to build a Roll-Up Summary field reaching directly from Project through to Employee, skipping Team Member
Doesn't recognize the junction object needs the data on itself for a standard roll-up to work
Doesn't propose an intermediate automation step when the data originates further away (on Employee)
Confuses lookup relationships with master-detail, assuming roll-up summary works on either
keyPoints: Correctly explains Roll-Up Summary's one-level, master-detail-only limitation
Correctly identifies Team Member (the junction object) as the field that must hold the data for a direct roll-up
Proposes an intermediate automation step when data originates further away on Employee
Keeps the chain of direct relationships intact rather than trying to skip a level

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the master-detail-only limitation of Roll-Up Summary fields
Correctly identifies where the summed field needs to live
Proposes a correct intermediate mechanism when data originates further away
Avoids an incorrect attempt to skip a relationship level

lessonLink.label: Review: Roll-Up Summary Fields and Junction Objects

questions.title: Writing a Cross-Object Validation Rule Formula
questions.prompt: A Quote Line Item should never be saved with a discount greater than the discount limit configured on its parent Quote's Account. Walk through the actual validation rule formula you'd write, including how you'd reach the parent Account's field from a Quote Line Item.
questions.modelAnswer: The formula needs to traverse two relationship hops from Quote Line Item: up to its parent Quote via the Quote lookup/master-detail relationship, and from Quote up to its Account via the Account lookup on Quote — in formula syntax that's Quote__r.Account__r.Max_Discount_Percent__c, using the relationship name suffixed with __r to dereference through a lookup rather than trying to query it separately. The validation rule's error condition formula would be Discount_Percent__c > Quote__r.Account__r.Max_Discount_Percent__c, which evaluates to true (blocking the save) whenever the line item's discount exceeds the account's configured limit. A few things matter in getting this right: the relationship chain only works if both relationships (Line Item to Quote, and Quote to Account) are actual lookup or master-detail fields, not just logically related data with no direct relationship field — if either link is missing, you'd need to add it before this formula is possible. I'd also add a null-check consideration: if Max_Discount_Percent__c can be blank on some Accounts, the formula should decide explicitly whether a blank limit means 'no limit' (requiring an ISBLANK guard so the rule doesn't inadvertently block everything when the field is empty) or whether a blank limit should itself block all discounts — that's a business decision the formula needs to encode explicitly, not something to leave as an accidental side effect of Salesforce's blank-field formula behavior.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a two-hop relationship formula, and the syntax for hopping through a lookup is just the relationship name with __r on the end instead of __c. So from Quote Line Item, I go up to Quote through its lookup, then from Quote up to Account through its lookup, which gives me Quote__r.Account__r.Max_Discount_Percent__c. The validation rule's error condition is just Discount_Percent__c greater than that value. The thing I wouldn't skip is checking what happens when Max_Discount_Percent__c is blank on some Account — because if I don't explicitly handle that, I need to know whether blank means 'this account has no discount limit, allow anything' or 'this account hasn't been configured yet, block everything.' Salesforce's formula behavior with blank numeric fields can surprise people here, so I'd make that decision explicit with an ISBLANK check rather than just trusting the default comparison behavior and finding out which way it actually went after someone hits it in production.
commonMistakes: Uses __c instead of __r when traversing the relationship, which fails as a formula reference
Doesn't address what happens when the Account's discount limit field is blank
Assumes the relationship fields already exist without checking both hops are actual lookups
Writes the comparison in the wrong direction (blocking the wrong condition)
keyPoints: Correctly uses __r relationship syntax to traverse two hops
Writes a correct error condition comparing the line item's discount to the account's limit
Explicitly addresses blank-field behavior on the account's discount limit
Confirms both relationship fields actually exist as lookups before relying on the formula

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly writes the two-hop __r relationship formula
Correctly explains the error condition logic
Addresses blank-field behavior explicitly
Confirms relationship prerequisites exist

questions.title: Modeling Custom Objects and Relationships for a Multi-Vendor App
questions.prompt: A custom app needs to track Purchase Orders issued to Vendors, each containing multiple Line Items referencing a Product Catalog, where a Product can appear on many different Purchase Orders across many Vendors. Walk through the actual object and relationship design.
questions.modelAnswer: Create a Purchase_Order__c custom object with a lookup (not master-detail, since a Purchase Order could reasonably need to exist independently or be reparented, and Vendor shouldn't be forced to cascade-delete every PO if a Vendor record were ever deleted) to Vendor__c. Create a Product_Catalog__c object holding the reusable product definitions, standalone with no dependency on Purchase Order. The relationship between a Purchase Order and the Products on it is many-to-many (a PO contains many Products, a Product appears on many POs), which standard relationship fields can't express directly — this needs a junction object, Purchase_Order_Line_Item__c, with a master-detail relationship to Purchase_Order__c (since a line item has no meaning without its parent PO, and deleting the PO should cascade-delete its line items) and a lookup relationship to Product_Catalog__c (not master-detail, since deleting a line item shouldn't delete the underlying product, and a Product's deletion shouldn't be blocked or cascaded by every PO that's ever referenced it — actually a lookup here that prevents deletion if referenced, via Salesforce's default lookup delete protection, is the safer choice and still correct). Quantity and unit price-at-time-of-order fields live on the junction object itself, since those values are specific to that particular line item, not to the Product Catalog record generally. This gives you a correct many-to-many model: Vendor to PO is one-to-many via lookup, PO to Line Item is one-to-many via master-detail, and Line Item to Product is many-to-one via lookup, together correctly expressing that any Product can appear on any number of POs across any number of Vendors.
questions.professionalAnswer: The many-to-many relationship is the part that needs a junction object, so I'd start there: Purchase Order Line Item, sitting between Purchase Order and Product Catalog. It needs to be master-detail to Purchase Order, because a line item genuinely has no independent existence — if the PO goes away, the line item should go with it. But it should be a lookup, not master-detail, to Product Catalog, because deleting a line item obviously shouldn't delete the product, and I don't want a Product's own lifecycle tied to however many POs happen to reference it — a lookup with Salesforce's standard delete protection is the right level of safety there. For Vendor to Purchase Order, I'd also use a lookup rather than master-detail, because a PO having an independent-enough lifecycle that I might want to reparent it to a different vendor, or not have it auto-delete if a vendor record were ever removed, feels like the safer default here rather than assuming master-detail is always the 'more correct' choice just because the relationship is hierarchical. Quantity and price-at-time-of-order belong on the junction record itself, not on Product Catalog, because those values are specific to that one line on that one PO, not a property of the product in general.
commonMistakes: Tries to model the many-to-many relationship without a junction object
Makes every relationship master-detail by default without considering delete-cascade implications
Puts line-item-specific fields (quantity, price-at-time-of-order) on Product Catalog instead of the junction object
Doesn't justify the lookup vs. master-detail choice for each relationship
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the need for a junction object for the many-to-many relationship
Correctly reasons through lookup vs. master-detail for each relationship based on delete-cascade implications
Places line-item-specific fields on the junction object, not the Product Catalog
Produces a coherent, correctly normalized object model

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the junction object for the many-to-many relationship
Correctly reasons through lookup vs. master-detail choices
Correctly places line-item-specific data on the junction object
Produces an overall coherent object model

questions.title: Implementing the Security Model for the LTV Customer Management System Capstone
questions.prompt: In the LTV Customer Management System capstone, you've already designed a security model on paper for the fictional company. Walk through how you'd actually implement it in the org: the order of configuration steps, and how you'd verify it matches the design before moving on to automation.
questions.modelAnswer: Implementation should follow a specific order because later pieces depend on earlier ones existing: first, create or confirm the profiles representing the distinct user populations the design calls for (minimal set, not one per nuance), then create the role hierarchy reflecting the actual reporting/visibility structure the design specified. Next, set organization-wide defaults for each object to the most restrictive setting the design calls for, since OWD is the baseline every other mechanism only adds on top of — setting this last would mean testing against an incorrectly-open baseline the whole time. Then build sharing rules and public groups for the cross-cutting access the design identified that role hierarchy alone doesn't cover, followed by permission sets for the finer-grained, composable variations on top of the base profiles. Only after all of that is in place would I move on to field-level security review (confirming it matches the design's intent per profile/permission set) and finally a Case/Account/Opportunity Team setup if the design called for record-level collaborative access. To verify this matches the design before moving to automation: create a small number of test users, one per distinct persona the design defined, and use Login As (or a documented walkthrough) to confirm each persona sees exactly the records and fields the design specified — not more, not less — documenting any gap between the as-built configuration and the original design doc so the discrepancy is explicit rather than silently accepted.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just start clicking through Setup in whatever order feels natural — the sequence actually matters because each piece depends on the one before it. Profiles and role hierarchy first, since basically everything else assumes those exist. Then organization-wide defaults, set to the most restrictive level the design calls for, because OWD is the floor everything else builds on top of — if I left that for later, I'd be testing against a baseline that's wrong the whole time and not even know it. Then sharing rules and public groups for whatever cross-team access role hierarchy doesn't cover, then permission sets layered on top of the base profiles for the finer access variations. Only once all of that's actually in place would I go back and double check field-level security lines up with what the design intended. Before I move on to building any automation on top of this, I'd create one test user per persona the design defined and literally log in as each of them, confirming they see exactly what the design said they should see — and if anything doesn't match, I'd write that gap down explicitly rather than just quietly patching it and moving on, because the design doc and the actual org drifting apart silently is exactly the kind of thing that causes problems much later.
commonMistakes: Builds sharing rules or permission sets before organization-wide defaults are set
Skips verifying the implementation against the original design doc, assuming it matches
Doesn't test from the perspective of each distinct persona defined in the design
Silently patches discrepancies between the design and the as-built configuration instead of documenting them
keyPoints: Implements in a correct dependency order (profiles/roles, then OWD, then sharing rules, then permission sets)
Sets OWD early as the baseline rather than leaving it for later
Tests from the perspective of each distinct persona defined in the design
Documents any gap between the design and the as-built configuration

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Implements in a correct, dependency-aware order
Correctly prioritizes organization-wide defaults as the baseline
Verifies the implementation against the design using persona-based testing
Documents discrepancies rather than silently resolving them

questions.title: A Recursive Flow Is Exhausting Governor Limits in Production
questions.prompt: Users report Opportunity saves intermittently failing with a generic governor limit error during business hours only. You suspect recursion between two of the twelve flows on Opportunity. Walk through exactly how you'd confirm it's recursion, identify which two flows, and fix it without disabling automation the business relies on.
questions.modelAnswer: First, reproduce the issue with Debug Logs enabled (Setup > Debug Logs, or the Flow's own interview history) on a user who hit the error, since 'intermittent, business hours only' strongly suggests a data-dependent recursion path rather than a universal bug — meaning it likely only triggers when a specific combination of field values is present, not on every save. The debug log's Cumulative Limit Usage section shows exactly how many times each flow/trigger fired within the transaction; if one flow shows an unusually high interview count for a single record save, that's the direct evidence of recursion. Cross-reference that against the twelve flows' entry conditions to find the pair where Flow A's after-save update to a field is exactly the condition that re-triggers Flow B, which in turn updates a field that re-triggers Flow A — this is almost always traceable by checking which fields each of the twelve flows' entry conditions reference against which fields each flow actually writes to, looking for an overlap between what one flow writes and what another watches. Once identified, the fix that doesn't disable business-relied-on automation is tightening both flows' entry conditions to the specific field-value transition that should trigger them (not a generic 'record updated'), which in most real cases breaks the cycle because the second pass's field value no longer matches the narrower condition. If that's not sufficient because the two flows have a genuinely circular legitimate dependency, add an explicit recursion-guard check (a flag field or a formula comparing old/new values) at the entry of one of the two flows as a more surgical fix, rather than disabling either flow outright.
questions.professionalAnswer: Intermittent and only during business hours tells me this probably depends on specific data conditions that happen to occur more during live usage than in whatever's running overnight, so the first thing I'd do is get debug logs from an actual user who hit it, not try to reproduce it blind. In the debug log, the cumulative limit usage section will show me if one flow is firing way more times than it should for a single save — that's the smoking gun for recursion, not a guess. From there I'm cross-referencing the twelve flows' entry conditions against what each one actually writes, specifically looking for the pair where one flow's output happens to be the other flow's trigger condition, and vice versa. Once I've found that pair, my first fix is always tightening both of their entry conditions to the exact field-value change that should matter, not 'any update' — that alone breaks most recursion loops because the second pass just doesn't match the narrower condition anymore. I'd avoid disabling either flow as a quick fix, because the business presumably needs both, and only if the two flows have a genuinely circular legitimate need to react to each other would I add an explicit guard flag to break the loop surgically rather than removing functionality people rely on.
commonMistakes: Tries to reproduce the issue without pulling actual debug logs from an affected user/transaction
Doesn't use cumulative limit usage data to confirm which flow is actually looping
Jumps to disabling one of the flows instead of tightening entry conditions
Doesn't explain why the issue is intermittent (data-dependent, not universal)
keyPoints: Pulls real debug logs/interview history rather than guessing
Uses cumulative limit usage data to confirm which flow is looping
Cross-references entry conditions against writes to find the recursive pair
Fixes via tightened entry conditions first, reserving a recursion-guard flag for genuinely circular cases

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Uses real debug data to confirm and locate the recursion
Correctly explains the intermittent, data-dependent nature of the bug
Proposes tightened entry conditions as the primary fix
Avoids disabling business-critical automation; proposes a surgical guard if needed

questions.title: A Field Update Appears to Happen Out of Order
questions.prompt: A Case has both a before-save flow that sets Priority based on Severity, and an after-save flow that sends a notification referencing Priority. Support reports that the notification sometimes shows the old Priority value, not the one the before-save flow just set. Diagnose what's actually happening.
questions.modelAnswer: This points to the after-save flow referencing a stale value because of how it was triggered or what data it's reading from, not an actual ordering bug in Salesforce's save pipeline — before-save flows genuinely do complete before after-save flows in the documented order of execution, so if Priority were set correctly by the before-save flow, any after-save flow on the same save should see the updated value. The likely real cause: the after-save flow isn't actually triggering from the same save that the before-save flow acted on — for example, if the after-save flow is triggered by a different field changing (not Priority or Severity) and it reads Priority via a Get Records call rather than from $Record, that Get Records call could, in some edge cases, be reading from a point in the process before the before-save update is fully visible to a separate query, or more commonly, the after-save flow's own entry conditions aren't actually scoped to fire on the same transaction where Severity changed, so it's running on a subsequent, unrelated save where Priority happens to still reflect an earlier state relevant to that specific update. I'd confirm this by checking the after-save flow's actual entry conditions and whether it uses $Record (reflecting the current transaction's values) versus a separate Get Records query, and I'd check the debug log's field history for a specific affected Case to see the actual sequence of value changes across saves, not just assume the two flows are reacting to the same single save event.
questions.professionalAnswer: My instinct is this isn't actually an order-of-execution bug, because before-save genuinely does finish before after-save runs on the same transaction — that part of Salesforce is reliable. So I'd go look at whether the after-save flow is really reacting to the same save as the before-save flow, or to a different one. The two things I'd check first: is the after-save flow reading Priority from $Record, which reflects this transaction's current values, or is it doing a separate Get Records call that could be reading from a slightly different point in time or a stale cached value; and are its entry conditions actually scoped to fire specifically when Severity changes, or is it firing more broadly and sometimes running on an unrelated save where Priority just hasn't been touched yet in that particular transaction. I'd pull the field history and debug logs on one specific Case that showed this problem and trace the actual sequence of saves and values, because 'sometimes shows the old value' usually means the notification flow is reacting to the wrong event, not that Salesforce ran things in the wrong order.
commonMistakes: Assumes Salesforce ran before-save after after-save, contradicting documented order of execution
Doesn't check whether the after-save flow reads $Record vs. a separate Get Records query
Doesn't check whether the after-save flow's entry conditions actually scope to the same transaction
Doesn't trace an actual affected record's field history/debug log before proposing a fix
keyPoints: Correctly rules out an order-of-execution bug as the root cause
Investigates whether the after-save flow reads $Record vs. a separate query
Investigates whether entry conditions scope the after-save flow to the right transaction
Traces an actual affected record's history before proposing a fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons that this isn't a true order-of-execution violation
Identifies $Record vs. separate query as a key investigation point
Identifies entry-condition scoping as a key investigation point
Proposes tracing a real affected record before concluding

questions.title: A Data Load Fails Intermittently With External ID Mismatches
questions.prompt: A nightly integration upserting Contacts via an external ID on Account succeeds most nights but fails on roughly 2% of records with 'no matching record found' errors, and the affected records vary night to night. Walk through your diagnostic process.
questions.modelAnswer: A varying, non-fixed 2% failure rate (rather than the same records failing every night) suggests either a timing/race condition between when an Account's external ID gets populated versus when the dependent Contact load runs, or data quality drift on the source side rather than a configuration bug, since a configuration problem would typically fail consistently or not at all. I'd start by pulling the actual failed records from several different nights and checking whether their Account's external ID field was populated in Salesforce at the time of the Contact load — if the ERP's Account sync and Contact sync run as separate, not-strictly-sequenced jobs, a Contact can legitimately arrive for upsert before its Account has finished syncing that same night, which would explain both the 'sometimes fails' and 'different records each night' pattern (whichever Accounts happen to sync slightly late that particular night). I'd also check for duplicate or blank external ID values on Account — if two Accounts somehow share the same external ID value (a data quality problem on the source system), Salesforce's upsert would correctly reject the match as ambiguous, and which Accounts happen to have this problem could shift as records get created, updated, or merged over time. The fix depends on which: if it's a sequencing/race issue, the integration needs an explicit dependency (Account sync must complete and be confirmed before Contact sync begins, not just 'probably finishes first'); if it's duplicate/blank external IDs, that needs a uniqueness/data-quality fix on the source system or a Salesforce-side validation preventing blank or duplicate values on that field going forward.
questions.professionalAnswer: A failure rate that's consistently around 2% but hits different records each night is the detail that tells me this probably isn't a broken configuration — a broken mapping would fail the same way every time. That pattern smells like a timing issue: if Account and Contact sync are two separate jobs rather than one guaranteed sequence, it's entirely possible for a Contact to try to upsert against an Account that hasn't finished syncing yet that particular night, and which Accounts happen to be running slightly behind would naturally vary night to night. So I'd pull failed records from a few different nights and specifically check: was the Account's external ID actually present in Salesforce at the moment the Contact tried to match against it? I'd also check for duplicate or blank external ID values on the Account side, because if two Accounts somehow ended up with the same external ID, Salesforce correctly refuses to guess which one you meant, and that ambiguity could shift as source data changes. Depending on which one it turns out to be, the fix is either making Account sync a hard, confirmed prerequisite before Contact sync kicks off instead of hoping it finishes first, or fixing a uniqueness problem on the source system's external ID values.

Doesn't check for a timing/sequencing dependency between the Account and Contact sync jobs
Doesn't check for duplicate or blank external ID values on Account
Proposes a fix without first confirming which specific root cause applies
