Investigates sync job sequencing/timing as a likely cause
Investigates duplicate or blank external ID values as an alternate cause
Matches the fix to whichever root cause is actually confirmed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons about what a varying failure rate implies
Investigates sync timing/sequencing as a likely cause
Investigates duplicate/blank external ID values as an alternate cause
Proposes a fix matched to the confirmed root cause

questions.title: A Sharing Rule Isn't Granting the Access Everyone Expects
questions.prompt: A criteria-based sharing rule was set up to share Opportunities where Region equals 'West' with the West Sales public group, but two members of that group still can't see some West Opportunities. Walk through your troubleshooting steps.
questions.modelAnswer: First, verify the two users are actually, currently members of the West Sales public group — not just that they were added at some point, since group membership changes or nested group structures (a group containing another group, containing the user) can be a source of confusion, and I'd check this directly in the public group's member list rather than assuming. Second, check whether the specific Opportunities in question actually match the sharing rule's criteria exactly as configured — Region might be a picklist with a value that looks like 'West' visually but is actually a different underlying API value, or the field being checked by the rule might not be the field actually populated on those specific records (a common mistake is a criteria-based sharing rule referencing a formula field that doesn't recalculate on existing records until they're touched again, so older records retain a stale value the rule never matches against). Third, confirm the sharing rule's access level (Read Only vs. Read/Write) is sufficient for what the users are trying to do — 'can't see' sometimes actually means 'can see but can't edit,' which is a different, often overlooked problem. Fourth, check whether a more restrictive mechanism is overriding this — Restriction Rules, if active on Opportunity, narrow visibility even within records a sharing rule would otherwise grant, and would produce exactly this symptom for a subset of users. I'd verify each of these against the two specific records and two specific users actually affected, rather than theorizing about the sharing rule's logic in the abstract.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd go concrete immediately rather than staring at the sharing rule in the abstract — pick the two actual users and the actual Opportunities they can't see, and check each piece against that specific case. First: are they actually, currently members of the West Sales group right now, checked directly in the group, not assumed from memory. Second: does the Region field on those specific Opportunities actually match the rule's criteria exactly — I've seen this break because the criteria was built against a formula field that doesn't recalculate on old records until something touches them again, so the field value technically doesn't match even though it looks right in a report. Third: I'd double check this isn't actually an edit-access complaint disguised as a visibility complaint — sometimes 'can't see' really means 'can see but the fields are read-only,' and the rule's access level might just be Read Only when Read/Write was expected. And fourth, if Restriction Rules are active anywhere on Opportunity, those can narrow visibility back down even after a sharing rule grants broader access, which would explain exactly this kind of partial, user-specific symptom.
commonMistakes: Assumes the sharing rule's logic is wrong without first checking actual group membership on the affected users
Doesn't consider a stale formula field value as a reason specific records don't match the criteria
Conflates 'can't see' with 'can't edit' without checking the actual symptom
Doesn't consider Restriction Rules as a mechanism that could narrow visibility after the sharing rule grants it
keyPoints: Verifies actual, current group membership for the affected users
Checks whether the specific records' field values genuinely match the rule's criteria, including stale formula fields
Distinguishes a visibility problem from an edit-access problem
Considers Restriction Rules as a possible overriding mechanism

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Verifies group membership directly rather than assuming
Investigates whether the specific records actually match the rule's criteria
Distinguishes visibility from edit-access issues
Considers Restriction Rules or another overriding mechanism

questions.title: Sharing Recalculation Is Taking Hours After a Routine Role Change
questions.prompt: A seemingly minor role hierarchy adjustment (moving one role under a different parent) is still running its sharing recalculation job six hours later, and users are reporting slow page loads org-wide in the meantime. Walk through how you'd investigate and what your options are right now, mid-incident.
questions.modelAnswer: First, check the actual scope of what moved — a role that looks small in the hierarchy diagram can still own or be positioned above a disproportionately large number of records if ownership is concentrated (ownership skew) under that branch, so I'd check how many users and how many records sit under the moved role and any role now newly above or below it, since recalculation cost is driven by records affected, not by how the change looks visually in Setup. Second, check Setup's background job/async monitor to see if this recalculation is competing with other large async jobs (a concurrent data load, another automation's batch job) for the org's shared async processing capacity, since two large jobs contending for the same limited async slots can each take far longer than either would alone — if so, and if it's safe to do so, I'd consider whether any non-critical competing batch job can be paused to free up capacity for the recalculation to finish faster. Third, I would not attempt to cancel the recalculation job if it's already significantly underway, since an interrupted sharing recalculation can leave share records in an inconsistent intermediate state that's worse than either the old or new correct state, and harder to diagnose afterward — the safer mid-incident move is to let it complete while actively communicating a status update to affected users rather than taking an action that risks compounding the problem. Afterward, the postmortem should check why a seemingly small change caused this (very likely ownership/record-volume skew under that branch) so future role changes of similar shape get flagged and scheduled for a maintenance window before being made in the future.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I'd check isn't the role hierarchy diagram, it's the actual number of records underneath what moved, because a role that looks small on the page can still sit above a huge concentration of owned records if ownership is skewed there — and that record count, not the visual size of the hierarchy change, is what's driving six hours of recalculation. Second, I'd check the async job monitor to see if this recalculation is fighting for capacity against some other large job running at the same time, and if there's a non-critical batch job I can pause to free up room, I'd do that. What I would not do, six hours in, is cancel the recalculation job — interrupting it partway through can leave share records in a genuinely inconsistent state that's worse than where we started and much harder to untangle afterward, so mid-incident my move is to let it finish and keep people updated on status rather than take an action that might make this worse. Once it's done, the real fix is in the postmortem: figure out why a change that looked small caused this, which is almost certainly ownership concentration under that branch, and make sure role changes of that shape get scheduled for an actual maintenance window going forward instead of made casually.
commonMistakes: Assumes the change was small because it looked small in the hierarchy diagram, without checking record/ownership volume
Attempts to cancel the in-progress recalculation job, risking an inconsistent intermediate state
Doesn't check for competing async jobs consuming shared processing capacity
No postmortem plan to prevent a recurrence
keyPoints: Investigates actual record/ownership volume under the moved role, not visual hierarchy size
Checks for competing async jobs consuming capacity
Correctly avoids cancelling an in-progress recalculation job
Proposes a postmortem addressing future role-change scheduling

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly investigates actual record/ownership volume as the real driver of cost
Checks for competing async jobs
Correctly avoids cancelling the in-progress job and explains why
Proposes a reasonable postmortem/prevention step

questions.title: Duplicate Rules Aren't Catching Obvious Duplicates
questions.prompt: Despite an active duplicate rule on Lead, reps keep creating new Leads for people who already exist as Leads with a slightly different name spelling and the same phone number. Diagnose why the current rule is missing these.
questions.modelAnswer: The most likely cause is that the underlying matching rule the duplicate rule references is using an exact-match algorithm on name fields (and possibly not including phone at all, or using exact match on phone too, which fails on formatting differences like missing area codes or punctuation), so a name spelled slightly differently, or a phone number entered with different formatting, simply never satisfies an exact comparison even though a human would obviously recognize it as the same person. I'd check the actual Matching Rule definition (not just the Duplicate Rule, which merely references it) to see exactly which fields it compares and which match algorithm (exact vs. fuzzy) is applied to each — Salesforce's standard fuzzy matching options for name fields specifically exist to handle spelling variation and should be applied to First/Last Name, while phone should be compared using a normalized/fuzzy approach that tolerates formatting differences, not an exact string match. I'd also check whether the matching rule is actually active (an inactive matching rule means the duplicate rule referencing it silently does nothing, which produces exactly this 'duplicates aren't caught' symptom with no visible error anywhere) and whether the duplicate rule itself is scoped to run on the record-creation paths reps are actually using (the standard Lead creation UI, but also any Quick Create or API path, if reps are also using a mobile app or a different entry point that might not trigger it the same way).
questions.professionalAnswer: My first guess is that the matching rule underneath this is doing exact matching on name and maybe even on phone, and exact matching just doesn't catch what a human catches instantly — a slightly different spelling or a phone number with different formatting fails an exact comparison every time, even though it's obviously the same person. So I'd go straight to the actual Matching Rule definition, not just the Duplicate Rule that references it, and check which algorithm is applied to each field. Name fields need fuzzy matching specifically to tolerate spelling variation, and phone needs some kind of normalization so '555-1234' and '(555) 1234' are recognized as the same number instead of two different strings. I'd also just sanity-check that the matching rule is actually active — an inactive matching rule means the duplicate rule referencing it does nothing at all, silently, with no error telling anyone, which is a surprisingly common and boring explanation for 'the rule isn't catching anything.' And I'd check whether reps are creating these Leads through a path — a mobile app, maybe — that doesn't actually run the same duplicate check as the standard web UI.
commonMistakes: Doesn't check the actual Matching Rule's algorithm (exact vs. fuzzy) per field
Doesn't check whether the matching rule is actually active
Assumes the Duplicate Rule's configuration alone determines matching behavior, ignoring the Matching Rule it references
Doesn't consider alternate record-creation paths that might bypass the check
keyPoints: Correctly identifies exact-match algorithms as the likely root cause for missed fuzzy duplicates
Checks the underlying Matching Rule's field-level algorithm configuration specifically
Checks whether the matching rule is actually active
Considers alternate record-creation paths that might bypass the check

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies exact vs. fuzzy matching as the likely root cause
Investigates the Matching Rule definition specifically, not just the Duplicate Rule
Checks whether the matching rule is actually active

questions.title: An Unhandled Fault Leaves Partial Data Behind
questions.prompt: A flow creates a parent Invoice record and five related Line Item records. When one Line Item fails validation, support finds the Invoice and four Line Items were created anyway, with the fifth missing, leaving inconsistent data. Diagnose why this happened and how you'd prevent it.
questions.modelAnswer: This happens because Flow does not wrap multiple separate DML statements (the Invoice creation, and then a separate bulk creation of the five Line Items, or worse, five individual creations) in a single all-or-nothing transaction by default the way a well-designed Apex transaction with proper rollback would — each Create Records element is its own DML operation, and if the Line Items are being created individually inside a loop rather than as a single bulk Create Records call on a collection, a failure partway through leaves exactly the partial state described: whatever succeeded before the failure stays committed, and nothing automatically rolls back the Invoice or the already-created Line Items. The first fix is structural: build the five Line Items into a collection variable in memory and create them with a single Create Records element outside any loop, which means either all five succeed or all five fail together as one DML operation — this alone would have prevented a partial 4-of-5 state, though the Invoice itself would still exist even if all five Line Items failed, since it was a separate, earlier DML operation. For true all-or-nothing behavior across the Invoice and its Line Items together, the flow needs an explicit fault path on the Line Item creation step that, on failure, deletes the already-created Invoice (a compensating action, since Flow doesn't have native multi-statement rollback), or the entire operation needs to be restructured as a single Apex action invoked from the flow that wraps both DML operations in one transaction with native rollback on exception, which is the architecturally correct fix for a requirement that's genuinely all-or-nothing.
questions.professionalAnswer: The root issue is that Flow doesn't give you one big transaction that rolls back everything just because something downstream failed — each Create Records element is its own separate DML, and if those five Line Items were being created one at a time inside a loop instead of as a single bulk creation, then whichever ones succeeded before the failure just... stay created, and nothing automatically undoes the Invoice either. Step one is fixing the obvious bulkification problem: build all five Line Items into a collection and create them with one single Create Records element, so it's all five or none of them, not a partial trickle. But that still leaves the Invoice itself sitting there even if every Line Item fails, since it was a separate, earlier operation — so if the real requirement is genuinely all-or-nothing across both, I need an explicit fault path on the Line Item step that deletes the Invoice it just created if things go wrong, as a manual compensating action, because Flow doesn't give me native rollback across separate DML statements. Honestly, if this needs to be bulletproof all-or-nothing, that's the kind of requirement I'd push into a single Apex action that wraps both operations in one real transaction with actual rollback on exception, rather than trying to simulate it with fault paths and cleanup logic in Flow.
commonMistakes: Assumes Flow automatically rolls back all prior DML in the same flow when a later step fails
Doesn't identify individual-creation-inside-a-loop as compounding the partial-failure risk
Proposes only a fault message without addressing the actual data inconsistency left behind
Doesn't recognize when the requirement genuinely needs Apex-level transaction control
keyPoints: Correctly explains that Flow does not automatically roll back prior DML on a later failure
Fixes the bulkification problem (single Create Records call for all five Line Items)
Proposes a compensating action (deleting the Invoice) for true all-or-nothing behavior
Recognizes when the requirement calls for an Apex-based transaction instead

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why Flow left partial data behind (no automatic rollback)
Fixes the underlying bulkification issue
Proposes a correct compensating action for all-or-nothing behavior
Recognizes when Apex-level transaction control is the right escalation

questions.title: An Approval Process Is Stuck With No Clear Owner
questions.prompt: A Quote approval has been sitting for two weeks with no action, and nobody is sure who it's actually waiting on. Walk through how you'd diagnose where it's stuck and the configuration gap that let this happen.
questions.modelAnswer: First, pull up the record's approval history (available directly on the record's Approval History related list) to see exactly which step the request is currently sitting in and who it was actually assigned to at that step — this tells you definitively who the ball is in whose court with, rather than guessing. The likely configuration gap, given that nobody even knows who it's waiting on, is that the approver assignment for that step was configured as a specific named user (rather than a role or queue) who may have left the company, changed roles, or simply doesn't check a notification channel anyone's monitoring, combined with no delegated/alternate approver configured on that user's record, and no escalation or reminder mechanism in place to flag a request stuck past a reasonable threshold. I'd fix the immediate case by having an admin with appropriate permissions manually reassign or approve/recall the stuck approval request so the business isn't blocked further. The durable fix: configure delegated approvers on every approval-eligible user going forward, assign approval steps to roles or queues rather than specific named individuals where the business logic allows it (so departures or role changes don't orphan a pending approval), and build a scheduled flow or report that proactively flags any approval request pending beyond a defined threshold (e.g., 3 business days) and notifies a manager, so this becomes visible long before it reaches two weeks.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't guess — I'd pull the record's actual Approval History, which tells me exactly which step it's sitting in and who it was assigned to at that step, full stop. Given that literally nobody knows who it's waiting on, my bet is the step was assigned to a specific named person rather than a role or queue, and that person's either left, changed roles, or just isn't watching whatever notification channel this uses, and there's no delegated approver configured to catch that gap. Immediate fix: I, or whoever has the right permission, reassign or manually process that stuck approval so the business isn't blocked another day over this. The actual fix, though, is structural — every approver in this process needs a delegated approver configured, approval steps should go to a role or queue instead of one named person wherever the business logic allows it, so a departure doesn't orphan a request, and I'd build a simple scheduled check that flags anything sitting in approval past a few days and pings a manager about it — because the real failure here isn't that this one approval got stuck, it's that nothing was watching for exactly this.
commonMistakes: Guesses at the cause instead of pulling the record's actual Approval History
Doesn't identify named-individual approver assignment as the likely root cause
Fixes only the immediate stuck record without addressing the durable configuration gap
No proposal for an escalation/monitoring mechanism going forward
keyPoints: Pulls the actual Approval History to see exactly where the request is stuck
Identifies named-individual approver assignment with no delegate as the likely root cause
Resolves the immediate stuck case
Proposes delegated approvers, role/queue assignment, and a proactive escalation mechanism going forward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Uses the Approval History to diagnose the actual stuck step/owner
Correctly identifies the likely root cause (named approver, no delegate)
Resolves the immediate stuck case appropriately
Proposes a durable fix (delegates, role/queue assignment, escalation monitoring)

questions.title: A Field Is Visible in the UI but Invisible to a Flow
questions.prompt: A record-triggered flow's Decision element always evaluates a custom field as blank, even for records support confirms have a value in that field when viewed in the standard UI. Walk through your diagnosis.
questions.modelAnswer: The most common cause of exactly this symptom — a field visibly populated in the UI but reading as blank inside automation — is that the flow is running in user context with field-level security enforced, and the running user (or the context the flow executes under, if triggered by a process that runs as a specific integration/automation user) doesn't have field-level read access to that field, even though the person viewing it in the UI does; Flow silently returns a blank/null for a field it isn't permitted to read rather than throwing a visible error, which is what makes this confusing rather than an obvious failure. I'd check the flow's own configuration for whether it's set to run in system context or in the context of the user/process that triggers it, then check field-level security and permission sets for whatever that actual running context is. A second, less common but real possibility: the field is being read via a formula or cross-object reference that itself depends on a value not yet committed at the point the flow reads it within the save order (if this is a before-save flow reading a value that an after-save flow on a related object would set, timing rather than permissions would be the cause) — but given support confirms the field has a value when viewed normally, the field-level security explanation is the first and most likely one to rule in or out before considering a timing issue.
questions.professionalAnswer: This exact pattern — visible in the UI, blank to a flow — is almost always a field-level security issue, not a bug in the field itself. Flow doesn't throw a loud error when it's not allowed to read a field; it just quietly returns blank, which is exactly why this is confusing instead of obviously broken. So I'd check what context this flow actually runs in — system context ignores field-level security entirely, but if it's running in the user's context, or in the context of whatever automation user triggered it, I need to check that specific user or context's field-level security and permission sets against this field, not against my own admin access, which almost certainly can see everything. If that checks out and the field-level security really is fine for the actual running context, then I'd look at timing instead — whether this flow is reading the field before some other automation has actually set it within the same transaction — but since support's already confirmed the field has a real value when viewed normally, my money's on field-level security being the answer here, and that's where I'd look first.
commonMistakes: Assumes the field itself or the Decision element's formula is broken without checking field-level security
Doesn't check what context (system vs. user vs. automation user) the flow actually runs in
Checks their own admin access to the field instead of the actual running context's access
Jumps to a timing/order-of-execution explanation before ruling out field-level security
keyPoints: Correctly identifies field-level security as the most likely cause of a silent blank read
Explains that Flow returns blank rather than erroring when access is denied
Checks the actual running context's access, not the admin's own
Considers a timing explanation only after ruling out field-level security

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies field-level security as the likely root cause
Correctly explains Flow's silent-blank behavior on denied access
Checks the actual running context's access rather than the admin's own
Appropriately considers and sequences a timing-based alternate explanation

questions.title: A Guest User Can See Data They Shouldn't
questions.prompt: A security review discovers that the guest user profile on a public-facing community page has edit access to a custom object that should be strictly internal. Walk through how you'd investigate how this happened and what you'd do immediately.
questions.modelAnswer: Immediately, given this is unauthenticated public access to internal data, I'd treat this as an active incident, not a routine finding: revoke the guest profile's access to that object (object permissions and field-level security) right away, before completing the full investigation, since every minute it stays open is public exposure, and only then investigate root cause with the risk contained. For root cause, I'd check the guest user profile's object and field permissions directly (Setup > Digital Experiences > guest user profile, or the standalone guest license profile) and trace how edit access was granted — the most common path is that a permission set or a profile-level change intended for authenticated community users was mistakenly applied to, or copied onto, the guest profile as well, or that the object's organization-wide default combined with a sharing rule inadvertently extended to the guest user's sharing context. I'd also check whether this was a recent change (via Setup Audit Trail) to establish when it was introduced and by what change, since that tells you whether this is a long-standing exposure (requiring you to assess what data may have already been accessed or altered by the public) or a very recent regression from a specific recent deployment. After containment and root-cause, the durable fix is a standing practice: guest user profile permissions should be reviewed as their own explicit, separate step in any access-related change to a community-exposed object, never assumed to inherit safely from authenticated-user configuration.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first move here isn't investigation, it's containment — this is unauthenticated public access to an internal object, so I'm pulling that edit permission off the guest profile immediately, before I've even finished figuring out how it got there, because every minute it's live is public exposure to internal data. Once that's locked down, then I dig into how it happened. The most common story I'd expect to find is that someone made a permission change meant for authenticated community users and it either got applied to the guest profile too, or got copied onto it by habit, without anyone specifically reviewing what the guest profile — which has no login at all — should and shouldn't see. I'd check the Setup Audit Trail to pin down when this change actually happened, because that tells me whether I'm looking at a long-standing exposure, which means I now need to think hard about what might have already been accessed or changed by the public while this was open, or a recent regression from a specific deployment, which is a narrower, less alarming problem. Either way, the fix going forward is making guest profile review its own explicit checklist item any time someone touches permissions on a community-exposed object — it never gets to just inherit from whatever authenticated users are allowed.

Doesn't check the Setup Audit Trail to determine when the exposure was introduced
Doesn't consider the possibility that prior public access/data alteration already occurred
No durable process fix proposed to prevent recurrence

Proposes a durable guest-profile review practice to prevent recurrence

questions.title: Bulk API Load Timing Out at Exactly the Same Point Every Night
questions.prompt: A nightly Bulk API job consistently fails around the 70% completion mark, every night, at roughly the same elapsed time. Walk through your diagnostic approach, given that it's consistent rather than random.
questions.modelAnswer: A consistent failure point (same percentage, same elapsed time) rather than a random one strongly suggests a deterministic resource exhaustion or a data-dependent issue tied to something specific in that portion of the dataset, rather than network flakiness or random infrastructure issues, which would more likely fail at varying points. I'd check first whether the job is hitting an API request/processing time limit (Bulk API batches that individually run too long can time out, and if the data is sorted or batched in a way that happens to put more complex or larger records in a predictable position, the same batch position could consistently hit the limit) — pulling the actual batch-level error from the job's results would show exactly which batch failed and why. Second, I'd check whether this coincides with a competing scheduled process — if another job, batch Apex, or scheduled flow reliably kicks off around the same elapsed time every night and consumes shared async/API capacity, this load could be failing not because of its own data but because of real resource contention with something else scheduled nearby, which is worth checking by looking at what else runs on that schedule. Third, I'd check the data itself in that batch position for something structurally different — more related child records tied to those specific parent records (more DML cascading from automation these records trigger), a data quality issue consistently located in that part of the source extract, or a lock-contention pattern (two concurrent processes both touching the same subset of records) that would consistently show up around the same point if the source data is extracted and sorted the same way every night.
questions.professionalAnswer: Consistent failure at the same percentage every night is actually the easier case to debug, because it rules out 'random network blip' almost immediately — something specific and repeatable is happening right around that point. First, I'd pull the actual batch-level results from the failed job, not just the overall failure message, because that tells me exactly which batch failed and what error it threw — a timeout on an unusually large or complex batch is a very different problem from a validation error on specific records. Second, I'd check what else is scheduled to run around that same elapsed time every night, because if there's a competing job eating shared async or API capacity right when this one's at 70%, that's resource contention, not a problem with this job's own data. Third, if neither of those pans out, I'd look hard at the actual records sitting in that position in the source extract — if the data's sorted the same way every night, whatever's consistently in that 70% mark might have more related records triggering more automation, or some data quality issue specific to that slice, and that would explain why it's the same spot every single time instead of random.
commonMistakes: Treats the consistent failure point as coincidental rather than a diagnostic clue
Doesn't pull the actual batch-level error details, only looking at the overall job failure
Doesn't consider competing scheduled jobs consuming shared capacity at the same elapsed time
Doesn't consider that the source data's consistent sort order could explain a consistent failure position
keyPoints: Correctly reasons that a consistent failure point implies a deterministic cause, not randomness
Pulls actual batch-level error details rather than the overall job summary
Investigates competing scheduled processes consuming shared capacity
Investigates whether the source data's consistent structure explains the consistent failure position

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons about what a consistent failure point implies
Investigates actual batch-level error detail
Investigates competing scheduled jobs/resource contention
Investigates the source data's structure/sort order as a cause

questions.title: A Validation Rule Blocks a Bulk Load That Worked Fine Manually
questions.prompt: A validation rule has worked correctly for years of manual UI entry, but a new nightly Bulk API integration is failing a meaningful percentage of records against it. Walk through what's actually different and how you'd resolve it without just disabling the rule.
questions.modelAnswer: The validation rule's logic hasn't changed, but the context it's being evaluated against has: manual UI entry typically populates fields in a specific order with defaults, required-field enforcement at the page layout level, and a human noticing and correcting an obviously wrong value before submitting, none of which apply to an API-driven bulk load, which can submit a record with a combination of field values a human would never have actually entered (a blank field the UI usually defaults, a value outside the range the UI's picklist would have constrained them to, or a record missing a related record the UI would have forced you to create first). I'd pull the actual validation rule's error message and condition, then look at a sample of the specific failing records from the integration to see exactly which part of the condition they're tripping — this tells you whether the integration's source data genuinely contains invalid values that should be rejected (meaning the validation rule is doing its job correctly and the integration's source data needs cleanup), or whether the rule's condition makes an implicit assumption that was always true for UI-created records but isn't actually a real business requirement for API-created ones (for example, a rule that assumes a lookup is always populated by the time of save, which the UI enforces via page layout but the API has no such constraint on). If it's the latter, the fix is refining the validation rule's condition to express the actual business intent correctly for both paths, not disabling the rule — disabling it would let through exactly the invalid data it exists to catch for manual entry too.
questions.professionalAnswer: The validation rule itself hasn't changed, but the context around it clearly has — manual UI entry has a lot of invisible scaffolding helping records be valid before they even hit the rule: required fields enforced on the page layout, defaults, a human who'd notice something obviously wrong. An API bulk load has none of that; it can submit combinations of values a person would never have actually been able to enter through the UI. So before I touch the rule at all, I'd pull a sample of the actual failing records and see exactly what they're tripping on. If the integration's source data genuinely has bad values — things that should actually be rejected — then the rule's doing exactly its job and the real fix is cleaning up the source data or the integration's mapping, not touching the rule. But if I find the rule is making an assumption that was only ever true because the UI enforced it structurally — like assuming a lookup is always populated by save time, which the page layout guaranteed but the API never did — then the rule's condition needs to be made correct for both paths, not just disabled. I wouldn't disable it either way; disabling it reopens the door to exactly the bad data it's there to catch for every manual entry too.
commonMistakes: Proposes disabling or bypassing the validation rule for the integration instead of diagnosing the actual cause
Doesn't distinguish between genuinely invalid source data and an implicit UI-only assumption baked into the rule
Doesn't pull actual sample failing records before proposing a fix
Doesn't consider that UI scaffolding (defaults, required fields, page layout) was silently doing work the API load doesn't get

Pulls real sample failing records before diagnosing
Distinguishes genuinely invalid source data from an implicit, UI-only assumption in the rule

Investigates real sample failing records before concluding

questions.title: A Scheduled Flow Silently Stops Running
questions.prompt: A scheduled flow that used to run nightly to update Contract Renewal statuses hasn't run in two weeks, with no error notification received by anyone. Walk through your diagnostic steps.
questions.modelAnswer: First, check the flow's own version and activation status in Flow Builder — a very common, easy-to-miss cause is that someone created a new version of the flow (perhaps for an unrelated fix) and the new version was saved but never activated, or was activated but the schedule itself needs to be re-triggered/re-saved after certain types of changes, silently leaving the old, now-inactive version as the last one actually scheduled while everyone assumes the latest edits are live. Second, check Setup > Scheduled Jobs (or Apex Jobs, since scheduled flows run as a form of scheduled Apex under the hood) to see if the job is even still listed as scheduled at all, and if so, check its last run time and status there directly rather than relying on absence of an error notification, since 'no error received' could mean either 'ran fine with nothing to report' or 'never actually ran,' and those look identical from the outside if nobody's monitoring actively. Third, check whether the flow's own entry/start conditions (if it's a schedule-triggered flow with a batch filter) are matching zero records lately due to an upstream data change, which wouldn't be an error at all — the job runs successfully every night, finds nothing matching, and does nothing, which from the business's perspective looks identical to 'it stopped running.' Fourth, check if the running user associated with the scheduled flow (the user who activated it, since scheduled flows run as that user) has had their user deactivated, license changed, or permissions altered, since a flow scheduled under a now-deactivated or restricted user can silently fail to execute with no alert generated anywhere by default.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first stop is Flow Builder itself, checking the version history, because the single most common way this happens is someone made an unrelated change, saved a new version, and either forgot to activate it or the schedule didn't carry over the way they expected — meaning the flow that's 'live' isn't actually the one anyone thinks is live. Second, I'd go to the actual scheduled/Apex jobs list in Setup and check directly whether this job is still scheduled at all and what its last run time was, because 'no error notification' doesn't actually tell me whether it ran successfully with nothing to do, or never ran at all — those look the same from the outside unless I check the job log directly. Third, I'd ask whether an upstream data change means zero Contracts actually match this flow's filter criteria lately — if so, the flow's running fine every single night, finding nothing, and that's not a bug, that's a business-side change nobody flagged. And fourth, I'd check the user this flow runs as — if that person's been deactivated or had their license or permissions changed, the scheduled flow can just quietly stop executing with no alert going out to anyone by default.
commonMistakes: Assumes absence of an error notification means the flow is definitely not running at all
Doesn't check flow version/activation history for an unintentionally orphaned new version
Doesn't check the actual scheduled job log directly in Setup
Doesn't consider the running user's status (deactivated, license change) as a cause
keyPoints: Checks flow version/activation history for an unintentionally inactive new version
Checks the actual scheduled job log directly rather than relying on absence of error notifications
Considers that the flow may be running successfully but matching zero records due to a data change
Checks the running user's status (deactivation, license, permissions)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Checks flow version/activation status as a likely cause
Checks the actual scheduled job log rather than inferring from notifications
Considers the 'running but matching nothing' explanation
Checks the running user's status

questions.title: Investigating a Suspicious Login Pattern
questions.prompt: Session monitoring shows a single user account logging in from two geographically distant locations within a short window, and from an unfamiliar device type. Walk through your immediate investigation and response.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd pull the Login History report for that user immediately, checking source IP, login type (UI, API, mobile), browser/device, and whether the session was flagged by Salesforce's own high-velocity or unusual-location detection, since the specific combination of impossible-travel-distance plus an unfamiliar device is a strong, concrete signal of credential compromise rather than normal behavior, and should be treated with urgency rather than dismissed as a false positive without verification. Immediate containment, in parallel with investigation rather than only after: I'd expire the user's active sessions (Setup > Users > Session Management, or the equivalent) to force a fresh login, and depending on severity, reset their password and/or temporarily deactivate the account while confirming with the actual user through an out-of-band channel (phone call, not email, since email could be compromised too) whether either login was legitimately theirs — for example, a VPN or travel scenario can occasionally explain what looks like impossible travel, so verification with the real human matters before concluding compromise, but containment shouldn't wait for that confirmation given the stakes. I'd also check what that session actually did — which records were viewed, created, or exported — via the Login History and, if available, Field Audit Trail or Event Monitoring, since knowing what a compromised session touched determines whether this is just a credential issue or also a data-exposure incident needing broader response. Longer term, I'd check whether this user has (and whether the org broadly enforces) multi-factor authentication and IP login restrictions, since MFA specifically would have prevented an attacker from completing a login even with a stolen password.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is one of those situations where I act first and fully confirm second, because the cost of being wrong in the cautious direction is low and the cost of being wrong in the other direction is a real breach. I'd immediately pull the Login History for that user — IP, device, login type — and in parallel I'm expiring their active sessions to force a fresh login and seriously considering a password reset or temporary deactivation while I sort this out. Then I'd call the actual person, not email them, because if the account's compromised, email might be too, and ask directly whether either of those logins was legitimately them — sometimes it really is just a VPN or a trip that looks like impossible travel, but I want to hear that from them before I conclude anything, not assume it. Once containment's underway, I'd dig into what that suspicious session actually did — what records it touched, viewed, or exported — because that's the difference between 'we caught a credential issue early' and 'we have an actual data exposure to deal with.' And after this specific incident is handled, I'd push on whether MFA is actually enforced for this user and broadly across the org, because that's the control that would have stopped this cold even with a stolen password.
commonMistakes: Investigates fully before taking any containment action, leaving a possibly compromised session active
Confirms with the user via a channel (email) that could itself be compromised
Doesn't check what the suspicious session actually accessed or changed
No follow-up on MFA/login restriction enforcement as a preventive control
keyPoints: Pulls Login History immediately to gather concrete evidence
Takes containment action (session expiry, possible password reset/deactivation) in parallel with, not after, investigation
Verifies with the actual user via an out-of-band channel, not email
Investigates what the suspicious session actually accessed, and follows up on MFA/login restriction enforcement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Gathers concrete login evidence promptly
Takes appropriate containment action without waiting for full confirmation
Verifies with the user through an appropriately secure channel
Investigates session impact and follows up on MFA/preventive controls

questions.title: A Security Audit Finds Profiles With Far More Access Than Anyone Uses
questions.prompt: A security audit case study reveals several profiles granting broad 'Modify All' and 'View All' object permissions that, based on actual usage logs, nobody with those profiles actually needs. Walk through how you'd confirm the finding and safely reduce access without breaking anything.
questions.modelAnswer: First, confirm the finding is accurate and current before acting on it: cross-reference the profile's granted permissions against actual usage data (Field Audit Trail, Event Monitoring login/API usage if available, or at minimum interviews with a sample of users on that profile about what they actually do day to day), since a permission that looks unused in a sampling window might still be needed for an infrequent but legitimate task (a quarterly process, an edge-case workflow) that simply didn't occur during the observation period — reducing access based on usage data alone, without confirming with the actual business process owners, risks breaking something that only happens occasionally. Second, reduce access incrementally rather than all at once: move the broad object permissions off the profile and, if any genuine use case is identified, grant that specific permission via a narrowly-scoped permission set assigned only to the specific users who demonstrated the actual need, rather than leaving it broadly granted to everyone sharing that profile. Third, roll this out through a sandbox test first with the actual affected users attempting their real workflows under the reduced permissions, and schedule the production change with a defined rollback plan and a announced window, so if something unexpected breaks, you can revert quickly and the affected users know who to contact rather than discovering silently that something stopped working. Fourth, treat this as the start of an ongoing practice, not a one-time cleanup — schedule a recurring access review (quarterly or semi-annually) so permission creep doesn't silently re-accumulate the same way it apparently did to create this finding in the first place.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I touch anything, I want to actually confirm this finding rather than act on a usage snapshot that might just be missing an infrequent but legitimate use case — a permission that looks unused over a few weeks might still matter for something that only happens quarterly. So step one is cross-referencing actual usage data with real conversations with people on that profile about what they genuinely do, not just trusting the logs in isolation. Once I'm confident it's really unused, I don't yank it from the profile and call it done — I'd move that broad access off the profile entirely, and if there's any legitimate edge case that did surface, I'd grant that specific need through a narrow permission set to just the people who actually demonstrated it, not broadly to everyone on that profile by default. I'd test this in a sandbox first, with real affected users actually running their real workflows under the reduced access, and roll it out to production with an announced window and a clear rollback plan, so if something breaks that I didn't anticipate, I can undo it fast and people know exactly who to tell. And honestly, the bigger fix is making sure this doesn't just creep back — I'd push for a recurring access review on a real schedule, because however this permission crept this broad in the first place is probably still happening quietly somewhere else too.
commonMistakes: Reduces access immediately based on usage data alone, without confirming with actual business process owners
Removes broad access for everyone with no path for a legitimate, infrequent edge case
Rolls the change straight to production without sandbox testing or a rollback plan
Treats this as a one-time cleanup with no recurring review process proposed
keyPoints: Confirms the usage-data finding with actual business process owners before acting
Reduces broad access while providing a narrowly-scoped path for any legitimate edge case
Tests in a sandbox with real users and rolls out with a defined rollback plan
Proposes a recurring access review to prevent future permission creep

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Confirms the finding with real usage context before acting
Reduces access safely while preserving a path for legitimate edge cases
Tests and rolls out the change with a defined rollback plan
Proposes a recurring review to prevent recurrence

questions.title: Architecting Automation Across 15 Objects Without a Recursion Minefield
questions.prompt: You're brought in to design the automation architecture for a new org before any flows exist yet — 15 objects will eventually need automation. Lay out the architectural principles you'd establish up front so the org doesn't end up with the tangled, recursion-prone mess these teams usually inherit instead of build.
questions.modelAnswer: The foundational principle is one-flow-per-object-per-trigger-context as the default: one before-save record-triggered flow and one after-save record-triggered flow per object, with internal Decision elements branching for different business logic, rather than letting multiple independent flows accumulate on the same object over time — this makes the dependency graph single-threaded and readable instead of implicit across N separate automations whose relative interactions nobody can reason about. Second, entry conditions must always be scoped to the specific field-value transition that matters, never a generic 'record is updated,' which is both a performance discipline and the primary defense against recursion. Third, establish a clear escalation path to Apex in writing before any automation is built, so the decision of 'flow or Apex' for a given requirement is made against a standard, not ad hoc per builder. Fourth, require every flow to have a populated description field and fault-path handling on every DML element as a non-negotiable before it ships, enforced via a review step, not left to individual discipline. Fifth, establish naming conventions up front (object, trigger context, purpose) so the convention exists before 200 flows need retrofitting later. Sixth, build a cross-object dependency map as living documentation from day one — which flows touch which related objects — so a future admin can see the blast radius of a change before making it, rather than discovering it through an incident.
questions.professionalAnswer: Since nothing exists yet, this is the cheapest point in the org's whole lifecycle to get this right, so I'd put a small number of hard rules in place before a single flow gets built. One flow per object per trigger context — one before-save, one after-save, branching inside with Decision elements — rather than letting flows accumulate one at a time as new requirements show up, because that accumulation is exactly how every tangled org I've inherited got that way. Entry conditions always scoped to the specific field change that matters, never a generic 'record updated,' because that's both a performance habit and the actual mechanism that prevents recursion. I'd also settle the flow-versus-Apex decision as a written standard before anyone builds anything, so that's not being re-litigated object by object. Fault handling and a populated description field are non-negotiable on every flow before it ships — enforced by an actual review step, not just asked nicely. Naming convention gets decided now, while it costs nothing, instead of retrofitted onto 200 flows in three years. And I'd start a living cross-object dependency map on day one, because the real value of that document is knowing the blast radius of a change before you make it, not after something breaks and you're reconstructing it during an incident.
commonMistakes: Doesn't establish a one-flow-per-object-per-trigger-context default before flows start accumulating
Treats naming conventions and documentation as something to add later once there's a problem
Doesn't settle the flow-vs-Apex decision as a written standard up front
No proposal for a living cross-object dependency map
keyPoints: Establishes one-flow-per-object-per-trigger-context as the default architecture
Requires scoped entry conditions as both a performance and recursion-prevention discipline
Settles the flow-vs-Apex decision as a written standard before building begins
Establishes naming conventions, fault handling, and a dependency map from day one

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Establishes a sound default automation architecture per object
Builds in recursion-prevention discipline from the start
Settles governance decisions (flow vs. Apex, naming) proactively
Proposes living documentation (dependency map) as part of the architecture

questions.title: Proposing a Declarative-Automation Standard Document for Leadership Sign-Off
questions.prompt: You've drafted a declarative-automation standard (naming, flow-vs-Apex rules, fault handling, review gates) and need leadership to formally adopt it as policy, not just as your personal preference other admins can ignore. What goes into that proposal, and how do you frame the business case?
questions.modelAnswer: The proposal needs to open with the business cost of the status quo in concrete terms leadership cares about, not technical elegance: time lost to debugging recursion incidents, the risk of a bad automation reaching production because no review gate exists, and the ramp-up cost every new admin or contractor pays trying to understand undocumented, inconsistently-named automation. It should then present the standard itself as a small number of concrete, specific rules (not a long policy document), each tied back to one of those costs — naming convention reduces ramp-up time, the review gate reduces production incidents, the flow-vs-Apex rule prevents rework from choosing the wrong tool. Critically, it needs an enforcement mechanism leadership actually signs off on, since a standard with no teeth is exactly as effective as no standard — this usually means making the review gate a required step in the deployment process itself (not a suggestion), with a named owner responsible for it. Finally, it should include a realistic adoption plan: applies to all new work immediately at no cost, with existing automation triaged and brought into compliance over a defined, reasonably-scoped timeline rather than an open-ended 'eventually.' Leadership sign-off matters practically because it gives the standard authority when another admin or a contractor pushes back — 'this is policy, not my opinion' is a very different conversation than an informal convention one person is trying to enforce alone.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd open with cost, not elegance, because that's what gets leadership's attention — how much time has actually been lost to recursion incidents, how many production issues trace back to automation nobody reviewed before it shipped, how long it takes a new admin to get productive in an undocumented mess. Then I'd present the standard itself as a short list of specific rules, each one tied directly back to one of those costs, not as a long policy document nobody's going to read closely. The part I'd push hardest on is enforcement, because a standard everyone's supposed to follow voluntarily is functionally the same as no standard — I want the review gate built into the actual deployment process as a required step, with someone specifically named as the owner of that gate, not just 'the team should probably do this.' And I'd be upfront about the rollout: new work follows this immediately, at zero cost, and existing automation gets triaged and brought into line on a real timeline I can commit to, not an open-ended promise. The reason I want this as formal policy rather than my own convention is practical — when a contractor six months from now wants to skip the review gate because they're in a hurry, 'this is adopted policy' carries a lot more weight than me personally insisting on it.
commonMistakes: Leads with technical detail instead of the business cost of the current state
Proposes a long policy document instead of a small number of concrete rules
No enforcement mechanism, relying on voluntary compliance
No realistic, scoped adoption timeline for existing automation
keyPoints: Frames the proposal around concrete business costs leadership cares about
Presents the standard as a small number of specific, justified rules
Builds in a real enforcement mechanism with a named owner
Proposes a realistic, scoped adoption plan for new vs. existing automation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Frames the business case in terms leadership cares about
Presents a concrete, specific standard rather than vague policy
Builds in a real enforcement mechanism
Proposes a realistic adoption plan

questions.title: A Framework for Choosing Flow vs. Apex at the Architecture Level
questions.prompt: As the architect reviewing automation proposals before they're built, design the actual decision framework you'd apply to every new automation request, not just a gut call case by case.
questions.modelAnswer: A workable framework asks a fixed sequence of questions in order, stopping at the first 'yes' that forces Apex: does the logic require transactional rollback across multiple objects that Flow's fault paths can't cleanly express? Does it require unit-testable logic for a regulated or audited process where test coverage and code review are a compliance requirement, not a preference? Does it need to be called identically from multiple entry points (a flow, an API integration, a batch job) where a single Apex class avoids duplicating logic across those surfaces? Does the data volume or complexity exceed what Flow's native bulkification handles cleanly, confirmed by an actual test against realistic volume, not assumption? If none of those apply, the default is Flow, specifically because it keeps the logic visible and maintainable by the broader admin team rather than gated behind developer availability. The framework needs to be applied consistently and the answer documented against the specific question that triggered escalation to Apex, both so the decision survives personnel turnover and so a later reviewer isn't stuck re-deriving why something was built the way it was. I'd also build in a periodic review: logic that was correctly built in Apex for data-volume reasons should be revisited if Flow's capabilities improve (Salesforce actively expands what declarative automation can handle), since 'correct when it was built' isn't the same as 'correct forever.'
questions.professionalAnswer: I don't want this decided by gut feel request by request, so I run every proposal through the same fixed set of questions, in the same order, and I stop at the first yes. Does this need real transactional rollback across objects that Flow genuinely can't express cleanly? Does it need to be unit tested because it's touching something regulated where that's a compliance requirement, not a nice-to-have? Does the exact same logic need to be callable from a flow and an API integration and maybe a batch job, where duplicating it three times in three places is worse than one Apex class? Has someone actually tested this at realistic data volume and found Flow's bulkification genuinely insufficient, not just assumed it would be? If none of those are true, it's Flow — that's the default, specifically because it stays visible and maintainable by every admin on the team, not locked behind whoever wrote the Apex. And I document which specific question triggered the escalation whenever something does go to Apex, because that answer needs to survive me leaving the project, and because what justified Apex two years ago might not still be true if Flow's capabilities have grown since then — I'd want this revisited periodically, not treated as a permanent verdict.
commonMistakes: Applies the decision inconsistently, case by case, with no fixed framework
Doesn't require actual testing at realistic volume before citing performance as the reason for Apex
Doesn't document which specific criterion triggered the Apex escalation
Treats a past Apex decision as permanent, never revisiting it as Flow's capabilities evolve
keyPoints: Applies a fixed, ordered set of criteria consistently rather than ad hoc judgment
Requires actual testing at realistic volume before citing performance/complexity as justification
Documents which specific criterion triggered an Apex escalation
Builds in periodic review as Flow's native capabilities evolve

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a consistent, ordered decision framework
Requires evidence (real testing) rather than assumption for performance-based escalation
Requires documentation of the triggering criterion
Builds in periodic review of past decisions

questions.title: Designing the Data Model for the LTV Customer Management System Capstone
questions.prompt: Walk through the data-model design decisions for the LTV Customer Management System capstone: a fictional mid-sized company needs Accounts, Contacts, Opportunities, and a custom object to track onboarding tasks tied to a won Opportunity. What design choices matter most, and how do you defend them if challenged?
questions.modelAnswer: Start from the standard objects rather than reinventing them: Account and Contact are used as-is since the fictional company's structure (companies and their people) maps directly onto Salesforce's built-in model, and Opportunity is used as-is for the sales pipeline, since custom-rebuilding either would duplicate native functionality (reporting, standard automation hooks, native integrations) for no benefit. The onboarding-tasks requirement is genuinely custom: I'd create an Onboarding_Task__c object with a master-detail relationship to Opportunity, not a lookup, because an onboarding task has no meaning independent of the won Opportunity that generated it, and master-detail correctly cascades deletion and lets a future roll-up summary (e.g., counting completed onboarding tasks) work. A record-triggered flow on Opportunity (after-save, since it needs to create related records) generates the standard set of Onboarding_Task__c records automatically when Stage changes to Closed Won, rather than relying on someone to create them manually, since the design should model the real business process, not just the data shape. If challenged on why this wasn't built as a checklist field instead, the defense is that discrete records support individual ownership assignment, due dates, and status tracking per task, none of which a single checklist field or a long text field could support, and that's a direct requirement for a real onboarding process with multiple people involved. I'd also defend the choice of master-detail over lookup specifically: a lookup would have allowed an onboarding task to exist without an Opportunity or be reassigned to a different one, which doesn't match the business reality being modeled.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by not reinventing anything standard objects already do well — Account and Contact map directly onto the company's real structure, and Opportunity is exactly what the sales pipeline needs, so those just get used as-is. The real design decision is the onboarding task object, and I'd build it as its own custom object, master-detail to Opportunity rather than a lookup, because an onboarding task genuinely doesn't make sense without the won deal that created it — master-detail also gives me cascade delete and the option for a roll-up summary later, like counting completed tasks. I'd automate the actual creation with an after-save flow on Opportunity that fires when Stage moves to Closed Won, generating the standard set of onboarding tasks automatically, because the design should reflect the real process, not require someone to remember to do this by hand every time. If someone pushed back and asked why this isn't just a checklist field on the Opportunity, my answer is that a checklist field can't hold individual ownership, due dates, or status per item — the second this needs to be assigned to different people with their own deadlines, it has to be real records, not a flattened checklist. And I'd defend master-detail over lookup specifically because a lookup would let an onboarding task float around without a parent Opportunity or get reassigned to a different one, and that's just not how this business process actually works.
commonMistakes: Rebuilds Account/Contact/Opportunity functionality as custom objects instead of using the standard objects
Uses a lookup instead of master-detail for Onboarding Task, missing the cascade-delete/roll-up implications
Doesn't automate Onboarding Task creation, requiring manual record creation
Can't defend the custom-object choice against a simpler checklist-field alternative
keyPoints: Correctly uses standard objects (Account, Contact, Opportunity) rather than rebuilding them
Correctly chooses master-detail for the custom Onboarding Task object, with reasoning
Automates record creation tied to the real business trigger (Closed Won)
Can defend the design against a simpler alternative with concrete reasoning

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses standard objects rather than rebuilding functionality
Correctly designs the custom object relationship with sound reasoning
Automates the object's lifecycle tied to a real business event
Defends the design against a plausible simpler alternative

questions.title: Designing the Security Model for the LTV Customer Management System Capstone
questions.prompt: The same fictional company has three teams — Sales, Onboarding, and Support — each needing different visibility into Accounts and the Onboarding Tasks tied to them, plus a VP role that needs to see everything. Walk through the security model design and how you'd defend each major decision.
questions.modelAnswer: Set organization-wide default for Account and the custom Onboarding Task object to Private, since three distinct teams needing different, non-overlapping visibility is exactly the scenario that calls for an active-grant model rather than an open default. Build a role hierarchy with the VP positioned above all three teams' roles, which gives VP visibility into everything through standard hierarchy access alone, no additional sharing rule needed — this is the cheapest, most correct mechanism for a 'needs to see everything' requirement when it maps cleanly onto an org-chart position. For Sales needing visibility into their own Accounts, that's native owner-based access plus role hierarchy for their managers, requiring no special configuration. For Onboarding needing visibility specifically into Accounts that have reached the onboarding stage (not all Accounts, and not Sales' earlier-stage Accounts), a criteria-based sharing rule on Account filtered to a stage/flag field, shared with an Onboarding public group, is the right mechanism since this is based on record attribute, not organizational position. Support needing visibility tied to active cases would similarly use a criteria-based or case-team-based mechanism scoped to Accounts with open support engagements. If challenged on why Onboarding didn't just get broader role-hierarchy access instead of a sharing rule, the defense is that their need is attribute-based (which Accounts are in onboarding) not organizational-position-based, and role hierarchy can't express 'only Accounts past a certain stage,' while a criteria-based sharing rule does this exactly and automatically adjusts as Accounts move through stages.
questions.professionalAnswer: With three teams needing genuinely different, non-overlapping visibility, I'm starting from Private on both Account and Onboarding Task — this isn't a case where an open default happens to be fine. The VP requirement is the easy one: position that role above all three teams in the hierarchy, and visibility into everything comes for free through standard role-hierarchy access, no sharing rule needed at all. Sales seeing their own Accounts is just native owner-based access. The one I'd spend real design time on is Onboarding, because their need isn't about where they sit in the org chart, it's about which Accounts have actually reached the onboarding stage — that's an attribute of the record, not a reporting-structure fact, so role hierarchy literally cannot express it. That's a criteria-based sharing rule tied to a stage field, shared with an Onboarding group, and it automatically adjusts as Accounts move through stages without anyone maintaining it by hand. If someone asked why I didn't just give Onboarding broader hierarchy access instead, my answer is that would either under- or over-grant — they'd either miss Accounts that just moved into onboarding under a different manager's team, or see Accounts that haven't gotten there yet, and neither is what the business actually wants.
commonMistakes: Gives VP visibility via a sharing rule or permission instead of simple role hierarchy positioning
Tries to solve Onboarding's attribute-based visibility need with role hierarchy instead of a criteria-based sharing rule
Doesn't set organization-wide defaults to Private given the explicitly non-overlapping team visibility requirement
Can't defend why a simpler mechanism (broader hierarchy access) wasn't used instead
keyPoints: Correctly sets organization-wide defaults to Private given the requirements
Correctly uses role hierarchy positioning for the VP's full-visibility requirement
Correctly uses a criteria-based sharing rule for Onboarding's attribute-based visibility need
Can defend each mechanism choice against a plausible simpler alternative

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly sets organization-wide defaults
Correctly uses role hierarchy for the VP requirement
Correctly uses a criteria-based sharing rule for the Onboarding requirement
Defends each design decision with sound reasoning

questions.title: Sharing Architecture for Two Business Units That Both Touch the Same Accounts
questions.prompt: Two business units within the same company — a hardware division and a services division — both sell to overlapping sets of Accounts, each needing to see the other's activity for cross-sell purposes but manage their own Opportunities and forecasts independently. Design the sharing architecture.
questions.modelAnswer: Account itself should likely be Public Read Only or even Public Read/Write at the org-wide default level, since both divisions legitimately need visibility into the same Accounts for cross-sell awareness — trying to wall Accounts off by division would directly conflict with the stated cross-sell requirement, so the right design leans toward shared Account visibility by default rather than restricting it. Opportunity, by contrast, should be Private at the org-wide default, since each division needs to manage its own forecast and pipeline independently without the other division's deals cluttering their view or reports by default. On top of that Private Opportunity baseline, Account Teams (or a criteria-based sharing rule keyed to a Division field on Opportunity, shared to each division's group) gives the cross-sell visibility back in a controlled way: a hardware rep can see that a services deal exists on a shared Account (enough for cross-sell awareness) without that Opportunity cluttering their forecast or pipeline reports, since visibility and reporting roll-up are different concerns — visibility doesn't have to mean the Opportunity data pollutes the other division's forecast numbers, which is usually handled by scoping reports to the user's own division regardless of what they can technically see. I'd also recommend a Division picklist or lookup field on Opportunity as the backbone both the sharing rule and reporting filters key off of, making the whole architecture legible and consistently enforced rather than relying on separate, potentially-drifting criteria in different places.
questions.professionalAnswer: The tension here is real — both divisions need to see the same Accounts for cross-sell, but they each want their own Opportunities to stay their own for forecasting. So I'd split the defaults: Account goes broad, Public Read Only probably, because restricting Account visibility would directly undercut the cross-sell requirement that's the whole point of this design. Opportunity goes Private, because forecast integrity matters and neither division wants the other's deals cluttering their pipeline view by default. Then I'd use Account Teams, or a sharing rule keyed off a Division field on Opportunity, to deliberately open back up just enough visibility for cross-sell — a hardware rep can see that a services Opportunity exists on a shared Account, which is exactly the awareness this is for, without that Opportunity showing up in their own forecast reports, because visibility and what counts toward your forecast are two different things and I'd keep report filters scoped to each division regardless of raw visibility. I'd build one clean Division field that both the sharing rule and every division-scoped report key off of, specifically so this doesn't turn into five slightly different criteria scattered across different rules that drift out of sync with each other over time.
commonMistakes: Restricts Account visibility by division, directly conflicting with the stated cross-sell requirement
Leaves Opportunity visibility wide open, polluting each division's forecast with the other's deals
Conflates visibility with reporting roll-up, assuming shared visibility automatically means shared forecast numbers
Doesn't establish a single consistent field (Division) that both sharing and reporting key off of
keyPoints: Correctly sets Account org-wide default broad to support the cross-sell requirement
Correctly sets Opportunity org-wide default to Private to protect forecast independence
Uses Account Teams or a criteria-based sharing rule to restore targeted cross-sell visibility
