questions.title: Gathering Requirements From a Stakeholder Who Didn't Actually Know What They Needed
questions.prompt: Describe a time you had to gather automation or data-model requirements from a business stakeholder who gave you a solution ('just add a button that does X') instead of a problem, and the solution they asked for wasn't actually going to solve their real issue.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer resists simply building what was literally asked for, since delivering a technically correct implementation of a flawed request still produces an unhappy stakeholder once they discover it doesn't solve their actual problem, and resists the opposite extreme of unilaterally deciding to build something different without the stakeholder's buy-in. It should describe a specific technique for getting underneath a solution-shaped request to the actual underlying problem — asking what happens today without this button, what specifically goes wrong, and what success would look like in their own terms, rather than accepting the proposed solution as the requirement itself. It should include a concrete instance where this surfaced a different, better solution than what was originally requested, and should describe how that was proposed back to the stakeholder in a way that respected their original framing rather than dismissively telling them their request was wrong. It should close with the actual outcome and ideally the stakeholder's own reaction to the better solution once implemented.
questions.professionalAnswer: An Operations manager asked me to 'add a button that lets reps manually mark a Case as resolved and send a closing email,' and I could have just built exactly that, but instead I asked what was happening today without it — turned out reps were manually closing Cases and then separately, inconsistently, remembering or forgetting to email the customer, and some customers were complaining they never heard back even though the Case showed as resolved internally. The actual underlying problem wasn't 'reps need a button,' it was 'customers aren't reliably being notified when their issue is resolved,' which a manual button, even a well-built one, doesn't actually guarantee, because it still depends on a rep remembering to click it and not fat-fingering the wrong email template. I went back to her with that framing — not telling her the button idea was wrong, but showing her what I'd found about inconsistent notification — and proposed an automated email alert fired the moment Case status changes to Resolved, removing the dependency on anyone remembering anything. She agreed immediately once she saw the actual gap laid out, and told me afterward that customer complaints about not hearing back basically disappeared within a month, which a manual button alone almost certainly wouldn't have fixed, since it would have had the exact same reliability problem as the manual process it was replacing.
commonMistakes: Builds exactly what was literally requested without investigating the underlying problem
Unilaterally decides to build something different without bringing the stakeholder along
Dismissively tells the stakeholder their original request was wrong instead of reframing respectfully
No concrete outcome showing the better solution actually solved the real problem
keyPoints: Resists building exactly what was literally requested without investigating further
Describes a specific technique for surfacing the real underlying problem
Proposes the better solution respectfully, keeping the stakeholder engaged in the decision
Gives a concrete outcome showing the real problem was actually solved

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Resists building the literal request without investigation
Describes a specific technique for surfacing the real underlying problem
Proposes the better solution respectfully, keeping the stakeholder engaged
Gives a concrete outcome demonstrating the real problem was solved

questions.title: Mapping a Process Before Building It, When Stakeholders Wanted to Skip Straight to Building
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time stakeholders wanted to jump straight into building automation for a process, and you had to make the case for actually mapping the process first, even though that felt like it was slowing things down.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer acknowledges the legitimate pressure to move fast rather than dismissing the stakeholders' urgency as simply wrong, and makes the case for process mapping in terms of the cost it actually prevents, not as an abstract best practice — specifically, the cost of building automation for a process that isn't actually well understood yet, which typically surfaces as expensive rework once the gaps become visible in production rather than on a whiteboard. It should describe a lightweight, fast process-mapping approach (not a weeks-long exercise that would validate the stakeholders' fear that this slows things down) and a concrete instance where that quick mapping exercise actually surfaced a real gap or edge case that would have been far more expensive to discover after automation was already built around a flawed understanding of the process. It should close with how the time actually spent mapping compared to the time it saved, making the case retrospectively provable rather than just asserted.
questions.professionalAnswer: A sales team wanted to jump straight into building an approval flow for a new discount-request process, and I understood the urgency — they were losing deals to slow approvals and wanted a fix now, not a planning exercise. I didn't tell them mapping first was just best practice; I asked for one hour, not days, to walk through the actual process with the two people who handled discount requests most often, specifically because I didn't want to build automation around a version of the process that existed only in the sales director's head and not in reality. That one hour surfaced something nobody had mentioned in the initial ask: there was an undocumented, informal escalation path for discounts above a certain threshold that went to a VP, completely outside what anyone had described to me as 'the process.' If I'd built the flow straight from the initial ask, that escalation case would have hit production, failed silently or incorrectly, and we'd have discovered the gap from an angry VP asking why a deal they should have reviewed went through without them — probably costing far more than the one hour spent mapping cost us upfront. I went back to the sales team with that finding specifically, showed them what the hour had caught, and after that nobody pushed back on a short mapping step before building again.
commonMistakes: Dismisses the stakeholders' urgency as simply wrong instead of acknowledging it's legitimate
Proposes a lengthy mapping exercise that validates the fear that this slows things down
No concrete instance of mapping actually surfacing a real gap
Doesn't make the time-cost tradeoff concrete or provable after the fact
keyPoints: Acknowledges the legitimate pressure to move fast rather than dismissing it
Proposes a lightweight, fast mapping approach rather than a lengthy exercise
Gives a concrete instance where mapping surfaced a real, costly-to-discover-later gap
Makes the time-cost tradeoff concrete and provable in retrospect

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Acknowledges the legitimate urgency rather than dismissing it
Proposes a lightweight, fast mapping approach
Gives a concrete instance of mapping surfacing a real gap
Makes the time-cost tradeoff concrete and provable

questions.title: Prioritizing a Backlog of Competing Dashboard Requests
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you had a large backlog of dashboard and report requests from multiple departments, all claiming urgency. How did you build a prioritization framework and communicate it back to stakeholders?
questions.modelAnswer: The answer should quantify the backlog problem — number of open requests, number of competing departments, and why 'everything is urgent' had become the default. It should describe a concrete prioritization framework rather than ad hoc judgment calls: scoring requests against criteria like business impact, number of downstream decisions affected, cost of delay, and build effort, and making that framework visible to requesters rather than opaque. It should show how the framework was communicated back to stakeholders whose requests ranked lower — specifically how the candidate avoided just disappointing people silently, by explaining the reasoning and giving a realistic timeline. Strong answers mention a lightweight intake and triage process (a backlog board, a regular grooming cadence) so prioritization becomes repeatable rather than a one-time exercise, and close with a measurable outcome: reduced average time-to-delivery, fewer 'why hasn't my request been touched' escalations, or higher stakeholder satisfaction with transparency even when their request wasn't first in line.
questions.professionalAnswer: I inherited a backlog of 47 open dashboard requests across six departments, each department insisting theirs was the most urgent, with no shared criteria for sequencing any of it. I built a simple scoring model with four weighted factors — number of people who'd use it regularly, whether it supported a recurring decision versus a one-off curiosity, estimated build effort, and cost of continuing to delay it — and scored every open request against it in a spreadsheet I made visible to all six department leads, not just my own team. I ran a 30-minute session with each lead to walk through how their specific requests scored and why, which let me say 'your request is real and matters, here's exactly where it lands and why' instead of a vague 'we'll get to it.' Two leads pushed back hard on their ranking, and in one case they were right — I'd underweighted a compliance-driven request from Legal that had a hard regulatory deadline I hadn't accounted for, so I added a deadline-override factor to the model. We moved to a visible Kanban board with a biweekly grooming session so this became routine instead of a one-time fire drill. Average time from request to delivery dropped from eleven weeks to under four, and escalations to my manager about 'my request is stuck' dropped to nearly zero because people could see exactly where they stood and why.
commonMistakes: No concrete scoring criteria, just 'we prioritized based on urgency'
Keeping the prioritization logic opaque instead of sharing it with requesters
Not addressing how deprioritized stakeholders were communicated with
Treating the first prioritization pass as final instead of being open to correction
No repeatable process established, just a one-time cleanup
No measurable improvement in delivery time or stakeholder satisfaction
keyPoints: Quantifies the backlog and the competing-urgency problem
Introduces a concrete, weighted prioritization framework
Makes the framework and resulting rankings visible to stakeholders
Shows willingness to revise the framework when a legitimate gap is found
Establishes a repeatable intake/grooming process, not a one-time fix
Gives a measurable improvement in delivery time or escalation volume

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Concreteness of the prioritization framework
Transparency with stakeholders about rankings and reasoning
Willingness to revise the framework when challenged
Repeatability of the process going forward
Measurable outcome
